#3142. Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Streaming Services

It's the latest streaming service to add American and British Sign Language options, making movies more accessible and enjoyable for a wider audience.

Apple TV is adding sign language interpretation for a handful of supported streaming titles, beginning with the Apple original film Being Heumann, which premieres on Friday.

With iOS 27.2, you’ll find new options for American Sign Language and British Sign Language within Apple TV’s app settings. When you select one of these languages, a new button will appear on supported Apple original titles indicating sign language availability. You can also turn off or change your language selection directly within the player.

Titles that support sign language interpretation will have a sign language icon displaying an image of a hand. This icon appears on the title page of a show or movie, next to other accessibility options like closed captions and audio descriptions.

Being Heumann is an apt pick for debuting this accessibility feature. The film centers on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and her leadership in the historic 1977 protest that helped advance equal rights and protections for Americans with disabilities. Sign language support will also roll out to other Apple TV titles starting with F1 The Movie, followed by Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid (which debuts Nov. 25) later this year.

Apple TV is adding a dedicated collection called Movies & Shows with American Sign Language to make it easier to browse supported content. That collection will include movies where sign language is part of the story, such as 2021’s Oscar-winning film CODA. You can also look up “with ASL” in the app’s search bar to find relevant titles.

“We believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, said in a statement. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences.”

Apple TV joins a handful of other streaming platforms with sign language options, including HBO Max and Prime Video. Netflix also features sign language interpretation for dozens of kids and family titles through a partnership with SignUp Media, which built a Chrome extension that overlays an interpreter onto supported shows and movies. SignUp is also available on select Disney Plus and Peacock content.

While closed captioning can help some deaf and hard-of-hearing people better understand what’s happening on screen, many viewers prefer watching with sign language interpretation, which can better convey emotion and expression.

“For the deaf community, our first language is ASL,” Nakia Smith, a deaf storyteller and an interpreter for the HBO Max series It: Welcome to Derry, told me in an interview earlier this year.

Unlike closed captioning, which has become nearly ubiquitous across streaming and television, sign languages like ASL are slowly making their way into more entertainment spaces, from sports broadcasts to awards ceremonies and red carpets. But there’s still a long way to go.

The challenge is that sign language interpretation requires skilled human professionals who can capture context and nuances, which takes time and resources. More companies appear to be making the effort. And while some studios are exploring AI to automate captioning, the complexity and diversity of sign languages suggest this will remain a largely human-driven endeavor for the foreseeable future.

For its part, Apple worked closely with the deaf community, partnering with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to ensure they matched the tone of the films and maintained authentic representation.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and who directed the film’s sign language interpretation, said in a statement. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

#3141. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3140. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

#3139. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: The AirTag for Android Fans

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google’s own tracker adds a few welcome details to the smart tracker field.

When a company comes out with its own version of a product in an established market, there has to be a good reason. Maybe it’s created a design that sets the product apart, or it’s included features that none of the competition has.

If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google is releasing the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available starting Wednesday for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a couple of days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

#3138. If the Tech Stock Sell-Off Turns Into a Bear Market, History Says This Investing Strategy Has Never Failed

The Nasdaq Composite is 11% off its recent high.

Tech stocks were routed last week after a blue wave in the midterm elections. There was plenty already bubbling beneath the surface, and a new government that could be hostile to tech growth set off alarm bells. Since peaking about a month ago, the S&P 500 is down almost 4%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) is down nearly 9%.

The tech sell-off could be a brief dip that rebounds to new highs, or it could turn into a bear market. In other words, no one knows what will happen next. While that's always the case, the underlying political and economic factors affecting the market are intensifying, increasing the likelihood of volatility and a market correction.

Investors who've never experienced this can feel fear, and even investors who have been there before can feel anxiety watching their holdings plummet. If you're not sure what to do right now, this one investing strategy has never failed.

First, a definition. Technically, the market turns bear when it's 20% off its recent high. When it happens, the worst thing you can do if stocks start to fall is sell. That turns paper losses into real losses, whereas if you hold on, the odds are that your stocks will rebound and go higher.

The last bear market was in 2022, and it lasted for most of the year. The Nasdaq lost 35% of its value in total by the time it bottomed out. Since then, it's up 150%.

What you need to do in a bear market is hold on to your stocks and wait it out. This is even more important when the market is volatile and could spring back up at any moment. It could rise again next week, but if you've sold, you won't get your money back.

Consider that history is on your side. In the 12 months following midterm elections going back to 1950, the S&P 500 has posted a gain every time, with an average gain of 15%.

Taking that a step further (back), since the end of World War II, the S&P 500 has delivered a gain 74.7% of the time. It lost value in consecutive years only twice (and once three years in a row), but it also posted gains of at least four consecutive years five times.

Holding on through the difficult years has led to fabulous wealth. And this holds whether investors have found the optimal time to invest or not.

For example, the investment company Charles Schwab studied five theoretical investors who had $2,000 to invest annually over 20 years. One had perfect timing; one invested on the first day of each trading year; another invested on the first of each month; one had exceptionally bad timing and invested only at market peaks; and the fifth shunned the stock market in favor of Treasury bills.

The investor who timed everything right had the best return with $186,000. But interestingly, the second and third investors did almost as well, coming away with $171,000 and $167,000. And the one with awful timing still walked away with $151,000.

The only investor who suffered was the one who skipped the market altogether; the Treasury bills generated only $47,000 over 20 years.

So, you don't need to time the market to benefit from its compounding over many years. If you invest consistently and tune out the noise about market ups and downs, your money can compound over time and grow into a solid nest egg.

One parting word: you can still make moves now to protect your portfolio during the rough years. If you're still loaded up on hot tech stocks, you may want to move some of your funds into dividend stocks and value stocks that can perform well under pressure. And if you might need some of your cash in the near future, it could make sense to sell a portion of your stocks before a bear market.

#3132. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

#3128. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

#3126. Amaero (AMRO) Q2 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Titanium output restarts as argon costs fall and defense demand builds.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Amaero Inc. (AMRO -13.63%) reported third quarter results that reflected a transition from facility build-out to commercial production scaling. Management stated that the company is currently focused on the simultaneous demand from several United States defense programs, including hypersonic weapon development and nuclear submarine construction. The company reported the successful restart of its titanium production lines following a safety review and the commissioning of specialized throughput equipment. Management indicated that the strategic focus remains on reshoring critical supply chains for high-value metal powders and near-net-shape components.

Operator: Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Shannon Devine, Investor Relations. Thank you. You may begin.

Shannon Devine: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining Amaero's third quarter 2026 earnings call. I am Shannon Devine. Joining me today are Hank Holland, Amaero's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Brett Paduch, Amaero's Chief Financial Officer. Earlier this afternoon, Amaero issued its earnings release and posted its earnings presentation, both of which are available on the investor relations section of the company's website. Before we begin, please note that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements regarding Amaero's business, financial performance, outlook, and future operating plans. Actual results may differ materially from those discussed today. Please refer to Amaero's earnings materials and SEC filings for a discussion of factors that could cause actual results to differ.

Any forward-looking statements that are made on this call speak only as of the date of this call, and Amaero disclaims any obligation to update any forward-looking statements, except as required by law. Certain non-GAAP financial measures will also be discussed. Information regarding Amaero's non-GAAP financial measures, including reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures, can be found in Amaero's earnings release and supplemental materials available on Amaero's investor relations website. With that, I will now turn the call over to Hank.

Hank Holland: Thank you, Shannon. Welcome. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us. Good morning to those joining from Australia. Welcome to Amaero's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call, and the inaugural earnings call as a Nasdaq-listed company. Our first earnings call as a Nasdaq-listed company also marks our first results reported in U.S. dollars under U.S. GAAP, so comparative figures may differ from those we previously reported on the ASX, where our CDIs continue to be quoted under the symbol 3DA. To our new shareholders, welcome, and thank you for your confidence. To our longstanding shareholders, thank you for your support over the past four and a half years.

Because many of you are new to Amaero, I want to begin with the bigger picture, the opportunity in front of us, why we believe that Amaero has a differentiated market position, and why we believe the company is at an inflection point. Then I will highlight the financial results in the third quarter and revenue guidance for the fourth quarter. Then Brett will take you through the financials in more detail. Amaero sits at the intersection of three enduring themes, rebuilding the U.S. defense industrial base, reshoring and scaling sovereign manufacturing, and the adoption of additive and advanced manufacturing. For the first time in decades, aerospace and defense are simultaneously experiencing peak demand.

The Columbia and Virginia-class submarine programs, the advent of hypersonic weapons, the replacement of the Minuteman ICBM with Sentinel, and the build-out of missile defense are driving generational investment. At the same time, the war in Ukraine exposed how thin our domestic capacity is in large castings and forgings, among the most constrained links in the defense supply chain. I want to emphasize all these themes are structural, not cyclical. The United States allowed its defense industrial base to atrophy over three decades. Rebuilding it and bringing critical supply chains home is both a national security imperative and sound economic policy. Amaero's corporate strategy has been driven by a demand pull that is a direct result of these thematic forces.

Within that backdrop, Amaero addresses two specific bottlenecks. The first in high-value spherical metal powders. Powder is the consumable of metal 3D printing, the ink cartridge to the printer. So as the installed base of metal 3D printers expands, powder demand expands with it. It is a pick-and-shovel business. Titanium alloy powders serve defense, aerospace, medical, and consumer applications. Refractory alloy powders, such as niobium C103, serve high-temperature applications in high-growth verticals that include the defense, space, and nuclear energy sectors. The second is PM-HIP, or powder metallurgy hot isostatic pressing, a mature technology that was developed over seven decades ago and has the benefit of military specifications and mature datasets.

Amaero's technical team has done much of the pioneering work over the past two decades for producing large, complex, near-net-shape parts as an alternative to constrained castings and forgings. We estimate the U.S. addressable market across our three product lines at approximately $737 million in 2026, growing to approximately $1.5 billion by 2030. That is large enough to build a significant business, yet specialized enough to attract limited competition, which supports a specialty margin structure. As the largest shareholder, that combination is the thesis that led to my investment into Amaero, and it continues to guide our forward-leaning strategy.

Amaero has commissioned the largest U.S. domestic production capacity for titanium and refractory alloy spherical powders, co-located with PM-HIP manufacturing in AS9100D-certified facility near Chattanooga, Tennessee. The competitive landscape is narrow. In titanium powder, our two primary competitors operate in Canada. We have no primary competitor in the United States. In refractory powders, we have one primary competitor. In PM-HIP, others make simple parts, but our proprietary know-how and experience with complex near-net-shape components is highly differentiated. Our advantage rests on three things that are difficult to replicate. First, technology and know-how. We operate EIGA Premium atomizers, a crucible-free process that the Air Force Research Laboratory has called the industry standard for reactive and refractory materials.

Equipment alone does not make commercially viable powder. Our technical team, anchored by Eric Bono, our Chief Technology Officer, has made modifications to the equipment and optimized the process parameters to deliver roughly twice the usable yield while consuming about half the argon gas of conventional atomizers. That matters because yield determines how much feedstock and labor go into every kilogram of sellable powder. Our two largest variable costs, and argon is a significant input of its own right. Our argon recycling system targets a further reduction in argon cost of at least 77%. Second, qualifications. The highest barrier to new entries and to production contracts.

Our C103 has been qualified to a manned space flight standard, and we've closely collaborated with the U.S. Navy, BPMI, and the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program for development, first articles, and qualification of critical submarine components. Third, customer relationships built on demand pull. Shortly after we moved to Tennessee, we committed to dedicating EIGA Premium atomizer to refractory alloys, including niobium, tungsten, tantalum, and molybdenum. This was a direct response to the long lead times from a sole supplier that was slowing down the development of hypersonic programs. Months later, we began close collaboration with leading stakeholders in Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, developed PM-HIP as a substitute for long lead time forgings.

Following a roundtable convened at our facility last December, the Navy's Maritime Industrial Base Program Office issued a formal letter of support validating our PM-HIP manufacturing as a viable and technically ready alternative casting and forgings. In July, we received our first low-rate initial production contract with BPMI. On the commercial side, we've structured long-term agreements with leaders in high-growth verticals, several naming Amaero as exclusive supplier. In July, we were awarded a $4.5 million Department of War contract to develop alternative refractory alloy powders that reduce cost and reliance on foreign raw materials. As other companies are beginning multi-year capital programs to address these bottlenecks, we have largely completed ours. Amaero is now shifting from build-out to scaling production.

Through September 30th, we had invested $52.2 million in plant and equipment. We operate three EIGA Premium atomizers with approximately 680 metric tons of annual capacity, 480 metric tons of titanium, and 200 metric tons refractory. Our fourth atomizer, expected in June 2027, takes total capacity to 920 metric tons. In August, we commissioned a custom-designed titanium sieving system that, together with our third atomizer, doubled our titanium throughput capacity. In our first full year of commercial production, the 12 months ended June 30th, we generated $12.5 million in revenue. Trailing 12-month revenue through September 30th was $13.5 million, up 191%, and our backlog as of September 30th of $13.4 million is roughly equal to that.

Because our fixed production costs are largely in place, we expect revenue growth to drive operating leverage. I also want to directly address safety. Following safety incidents earlier this year, we committed to lean in. We paused titanium production and completed a comprehensive process, system, and facility safety review with Jensen Hughes, a leader in safety, dust hazard, and risk-based engineering. We engaged Jensen Hughes to identify risk mitigation strategies that were utilized by larger-scale industrial operations with dust hazards, such as the sugar industry, paper mills, and grain operations. We implemented resulting improvements, and titanium production resumed in late July after approximately a six-week pause. No order cancellations and no employee attrition.

As for Q3 highlights and outlook, turning to the quarter. Third quarter revenue grew 35% to $4.1 million, landing near the top of the previously disclosed range, and nine-month revenue grew 170% to $11.5 million. We ended the period with a backlog of $13.4 million, an increase of 180% from September 2025, and approximately 100% of trailing 12-month revenue. Operating cash use for the quarter fell $1 million year-over-year to $6.3 million. Commercially, the Department of War award and our first BPMI contract advanced both of our production lines in defense, refractory powders and PM-HIP. Operationally, we restarted titanium production and doubled titanium throughput capacity with commissioning an expanded custom-designed fabricated sieving system.

In the capital markets, we began trading on Nasdaq on October 15, receiving aggregate net IPO proceeds of $17.0 million, and amended our EXIM Bank credit agreement to release $2.1 million of restricted cash and move the liquidity covenant test to 2028. As of October 31, we had $19.3 million of cash and cash equivalents after October operating cash use and capital expenditures. Today, we are issuing our first formal guidance as a U.S. listed company. We expect Q4 2026 revenue of $4.5 million-$5.0 million, which would result in a quarterly increase of 121%-146% year-over-year. Combined with our results to date, that would result in full year 2026 revenue of $16.0 million-$16.5 million, up 154%-162%.

Our priorities are clear, convert backlog into revenue, expand the breadth and depth of our commercial partnerships, and bring argon recycling and our fourth atomizer online in the first half of 2027. With that, I will turn it over to our CFO, Brett, to provide more detail on our financial results.

Brett Paduch: Thank you, Hank, and good afternoon. I will start by tying our actual financial results back to our previously disclosed ranges and to provide more detail to our financial performance. Revenue of $4.11 million was near the top end of $3.96 million-$4.12 million range. Cash of $4.96 million and backlog of $13.44 million landed within the range. Net loss attributable to stockholders of $9.06 million, operating cash use of $6.34 million, and Adjusted EBITDA of $-7.11 million all came in modestly favorable to the range. Turning to revenue. Q3 revenue rose 35% to $4.1 million, with growth in both product lines.

Metal powders contributed $3.2 million, up 19%, reflecting the continued ramp of our atomization capacity and the expansion of new and existing customer relationships. PM-HIP contributed $0.9 million, up 146%, including the first revenue attributable to our LRIP contract with BPMI. Looking beyond any single quarter, nine-month revenue through Q3 grew 170% to $11.5 million from $4.3 million, and trailing 12-month revenue grew 191% to $13.5 million from $4.7 million. Backlog as of September 30th of $13.4 million is up 34% from $10 million at June 30th, up 96% from $6.9 million at year-end 2025, and up 180% from $4.8 million a year ago.

It includes $4.4 million attributable to the Department of War development contract, and it spans both powder and PM-HIP. Turning to the income statement. Cost of revenue in Q3 was $8.5 million compared with $3.1 million in Q3 2025, resulting in a gross loss for Q3 2026 of $4.4 million. I want to be clear about what drove that. The increase reflects the continued scale-up of our Tennessee operations together with titanium production in the quarter running below installed capacity, first because of the restart in late July, and then because optimizing the new sieving system reduced throughput and yields.

As a result, our portion of production labor and fixed production costs were not absorbed into inventory and were expensed in the period, and lower yields increased the cost of titanium powder sold. Our fixed production costs consisted principally of plant salaried labor and overhead, depreciation on manufacturing equipment and leasehold improvements, and the lease on our Tennessee facility. With the equipment and the plant operating and technical teams for both product lines largely in place, we do not expect those costs to increase in proportion to revenue. That is why we expect revenue growth to drive continued operating leverage and gross margin improvement. SG&A in Q3 was $4.3 million, up $0.5 million compared to the prior year period.

The increase reflects $0.6 million of non-ordinary course redomiciliation and IPO-related costs, primarily legal, tax, and audit fees, together with higher corporate legal and audit fees, partially offset by $0.5 million decrease in stock-based compensation. Q3 R&D was $0.1 million. Loss from operations was $8.8 million, and net loss attributable to stockholders was $9.1 million, or $0.38 per share, compared to $4.1 million, or $0.20 per share, in the prior year period. Adjusted EBITDA in Q3, which excludes stock-based compensation of $0.3 million and $0.6 million of redomiciliation and IPO-related costs, was negative $7.1 million compared with negative $3.1 million in Q3 2025.

For the nine months ending September 30th, 2026, revenue grew 170% from the prior year period to $11.5 million, and Adjusted EBITDA was $-15.6 million versus $-10.7 million in the prior year period. Let me close with four takeaways. First, quarterly revenue grew 35% year-over-year. Second, forward visibility has improved. Backlog at quarter end was 2.8x its level a year earlier, and our guidance implies full-year revenue growth of 154%-162%. Third, with our fixed production cost base largely in place and titanium throughput capacity doubled, we expect higher titanium output to drive operating leverage and gross margin improvement.

Fourth, our next capacity additions, argon recycling in the first quarter of 2027 and our fourth EIGA atomizer in June 2027, remain on schedule, funded in part by our IPO proceeds. I'll turn it back to Hank.

Hank Holland: Thank you, Brett. Let me close where I began, the themes behind our business, rebuilding the defense industrial base, reshoring sovereign manufacturing, and the adoption of additive manufacturing. These are enduring, and Amaero is positioned at their intersection. Our foundational build-out is complete. Our capacity is commissioned and AS9100D certified. The qualifications, the highest barrier in this industry, are well advanced. PM-HIP has moved into production for the submarine industrial base, and our Department of War program is advancing. Revenue is ramping against a backlog equal to a full year of trailing revenue. Our job now is execution. Continue to scale production, convert backlog into revenue, bring argon recycling, our fourth atomizer, online the first half of 2027.

We believe this is how we build durable value for shareholders and make a durable contribution to U.S. national security. Thank you for your time today. Brett and I are happy to take your questions.

Operator: Thank you. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Our first question is from Peter Arment with Baird. Please proceed.

Peter Arment: Yeah. Good afternoon, Hank and Brett. Nice results. Hey, Hank, good to see titanium process restarted. Could you maybe talk about just how you're seeing the process, have things stabilized, and then is the new sieving system fully optimized? How we should be thinking about any remaining bottlenecks there?

Hank Holland: Yeah, absolutely. Thank you very much, Peter. As you've seen firsthand, the sieving system that we installed, we believe to be the largest system of its type in the world outside of China for reactive metals. The sieving is the bottleneck process of powder production. As you stated, we restarted titanium production the end of July, and that has gone quite well. We had already commissioned the third atomizer, the second dedicated titanium in June. Then in the month of August is when we commissioned the sieving system. I would say that by the time we got into early to mid-September, most of the parameter optimization was dialed in.

We're continuing to make small tweaks, and I would expect that through the very end of this year, we'll be making small tweaks. I would say from a yield standpoint, the yield was below optimal for last quarter, and I would expect this quarter, over the course of the quarter, we will begin to approach where we would expect it to be longer term.

Peter Arment: Got it. That's helpful. Brett, a quick one on, I know you're not guiding to gross margins or anything for Q4, but just given that maybe some of these startup or restart costs maybe are a little bit behind you, should we expect to see some of that leverage begin to show up here in Q4?

Brett Paduch: Yeah, I would say the fixed cost in our cost of goods sold is significantly scaled at this point. That includes both the rent, depreciation, it includes our technical and operating teams. So, as our revenue grows into Q4 and beyond, we would not expect a commensurate rise in those fixed production costs, which is where we would start seeing that operating leverage lead to improvement in our gross margin moving forward.

Hank Holland: Peter, the one thing that I would add, what Brett said, which is exactly right, the other thing is there tends to be about a six-week lag of inventory. The inventory cost that will come into Q4 of this, the current quarter that we are in, there will be a number of weeks of that inventory from last quarter that will be impacted by some of the same issues from yields and so forth. I would expect to see an improvement in gross margin, but we really will not begin to see the favorable trend as we would expect until we get into the next calendar year because of that modest lag.

Peter Arment: Okay. Just a quick one, just regarding your backlog. Is there anything that is unfunded as we are still in a continuing resolution in the U.S. for FY 2027, or do you have all the funding you need for what is in backlog?

Hank Holland: Yeah, I will take that briefly. All of the backlog as reported is contracted firm orders, all of which is expected to be recognized prior to June 30th, with the exception of there are two payments on the Department of War contract that I believe total about $700,000. Most of that backlog will be recognized before June 30th, all of which are firm commitments and all of which funding is in place. I will tell you that obviously none of us know exactly what will happen with the FY 2027 defense appropriation budget, particularly given the midterm elections, when that might be approved.

I would not see it having an impact on us so long as we eventually got the FY 2027 budget approved, i.e., even if it was in February or March of next year. We have got a significant pipeline of opportunities that have already received funding at our tier one supplier level. I would not expect any CR in the short term to impact what we see in calendar year 2027 or first half of calendar year 2027 revenues.

Peter Arment: Appreciate all the details, guys. I'll jump back in the queue. Thanks, Hank.

Operator: Our next question is from Jaeson Schmidt with Lake Street Capital Markets. Please proceed.

Jaeson Schmidt: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my questions, and congrats on the solid results. Sticking with backlog, I know you mentioned it spans both businesses. Just curious, if outside the DoW contract, are there any sort of larger, chunkier awards within that, or is it pretty broad-based across the diverse customer base?

Hank Holland: Yeah, I'll take that to start. The DoW award, as we've announced, was about $4.5 million, and so that is a chunk of that $13.4 million backlog. Beyond that, we do have long-term agreements in place, as in 12-month purchase orders. Keep in mind, Jaeson, that prior to the redomiciliation, our fiscal year ended June 30th, and so many of those 12-month POs had been structured from a July to June basis. So by the time we get through the end of December, we will have burnt off half of that 12-month PO. We'll obviously begin to restructure those on a going-forward basis, more so on a calendar year basis.

I think the other interesting thing, as you know, we announced back in July, I believe it was, the contract with BPMI. It was our first LRIP, or low-rate production contract. It was not a particularly large contract, about $350,000. However, it was a very important contract in that it was our first production. It was the seventh contract we had with BPMI, albeit the first one that we announced. And what we would now expect to see is that opens the door to a series of production contracts to follow. They're not yet showing up in backlog. They're showing up essentially in our pipeline.

But I would expect to see some relatively chunky orders that will follow in the PM-HIP business over time. The rest of it, again, I would say would be ordinary course of business, either spot orders or relatively short-term orders that we have in coupled with the Department of War contract.

Jaeson Schmidt: Got you. That's really helpful. And, Hank, my next question was going to be on BPMI and when we could see some production contracts. Any sense on the timeline there?

Hank Holland: Yeah, we're not in a position to say much more. A, we haven't given any guidance on that, and B, Jaeson, as you can appreciate, a lot of times the approval of these contracts take on kind of a life of their own, and we're always very, very mindful to be conservative with any guidance that we give. We do think that the announcement of the BPMI contract was quite consequential and does now position us for a series of contracts to follow. That's probably all we can say at this point, though.

Jaeson Schmidt: Okay. Makes sense. Thanks a lot, guys.

Operator: Our next question is from Doug Smith with Curran & Company. Please proceed.

Doug Smith: Hi, Hank. Hi, Brett. Congrats on the first U.S. quarterly report. I thought I'd ask about the backlog as well, and I've seen some news flow regarding hypersonic programs moving forward. Are you seeing some C103 signals start to come through related to [Castheon]? Also, what's the inbound sort of look like on the titanium, and how do we see that growing as we go forward?

Hank Holland: Yeah, so beginning with C103, this is one of the areas, as you well know, Doug, and that you've followed the company for quite some time, the FY 2025 CR and the subsequent government shutdown had a real impact on Amaero in delaying the revenue. Some of the C103 programs, I think about certain strategic missile programs, for example, were significantly impacted, and we're only now seeing some of those programs down select from what was probably as much as a two-year delay. Yes, we are seeing an uptick in C103 demand from defense applications. We're also seeing it on the space side.

As you know, in the case of niobium C103, first used in the Apollo lunar landing vehicle in 1969, it's really become the go-to high-temperature alloy. Where we have mission-critical applications, and whether that's particularly sensitive defense applications and/or space, it does seem to be the go-to alloy. I will tell you, part of what's exciting about our Department of War contract, though, is, as you well know, Doug, that one of the challenges with niobium C103, it's comprised 10% of hafnium, and hafnium prices are up about 700% the last several years.

The Department of War is anxious to find alternatives in the refractory high-temperature alloy space that do not include hafnium, and that's really where our program, the DoW, is focused. Yes, we are seeing uptick in demand for C103, but importantly, we're also seeing uptick in demand in alternative refractories as well.

Doug Smith: Okay, fantastic. Thanks for that, Hank. That is all for me.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question and answer session. This will conclude today's conference. You may disconnect your lines at this time, and thank you for your participation.

#3125. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.
