#3122. Hornbeck Offshore (HOS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First full quarter after the Helix merger shows a $1.9 billion backlog.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hornbeck Offshore Services, Inc. (HOS -2.97%) reported its first financial results following the Sept. 1 completion of its combination with Helix, establishing a diversified platform across marine transportation, subsea services, and well intervention. Management indicated the transaction enables the company to participate across the full offshore project life cycle, from development through decommissioning. The combined entity is pursuing an integrated services strategy, aiming to capture higher margins by bundling vessel, robotics, and engineering capabilities. Management issued full-year 2027 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $500 million to $550 million, supported by a $1.9 billion contracted backlog and the expected delivery of two high-specification newbuild vessels starting in late 2027.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Hornbeck Offshore Services Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Today's call is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Potter Adams, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead, sir.

Robert Adams: Thanks, operator, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us for Hornbeck Offshore's conference call to review our third quarter 2026 results and recent developments. We also welcome participants listening to the call over the web. Joining me on the call today is Todd Hornbeck, President and Chief Executive Officer of Hornbeck Offshore. Please note that information reported on this call speaks only as of today, November 5, 2026, and therefore, you are advised that time-sensitive information may no longer be accurate as of the time of any replay listening or transcript reading.

During today's conference call, Todd and I will make certain projections about future financial performance, liquidity, operations and events that are not statements of historical fact and thus constitute forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors that may cause such future matters, including the company's actual future performance to be materially different from that which is projected today. You can locate additional information about factors that could cause the company's results to materially differ from those projected in the forward-looking statements in Hornbeck's SEC filings and in yesterday's press release under the Investors section of the company's website, which is www.hornbeckoffshore.com or through the SEC website at www.sec.gov.

The earnings call also contains references to adjusted EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow, which are non-GAAP financial measures. A reconciliation of these financial measures is provided in the press release issued by the company yesterday afternoon. And finally, please note that the company uses its website as a means of disclosing material and other public information and for complying with disclosure obligations under SEC's Regulation FD. Such disclosures will be included on the company's website under the heading Investors. Accordingly, investors should monitor that portion of the company's website in addition to following the company's press releases, SEC filings, public conference calls and website. Now I'll turn the call over to Todd. Todd?

Todd Hornbeck: Thanks, Potter, and good morning, everyone. We thank you for joining us. This is an important quarter for Hornbeck as it marks our first earnings call following the completion of our combination with Helix on September 1. The transaction brought together 2 organizations with complementary assets, capabilities, talent and customer relationships. More details around the transaction can be found in the slides posted to our website. Potter will share some additional details later in his remarks. When we announced the combination in late April, we said we saw an opportunity to create a premier integrated offshore service company providing innovative marine and subsea solutions across deepwater oilfield, defense and renewable industries. This thesis has not changed.

What has changed is that we're now successfully executing it. Before we get to the results, I'd like to spend a moment discussing 3 key questions that we believe are most important to our shareholders. First, what exactly is the combined Hornbeck Offshore. Second, how does bringing these 2 businesses together create significant value. And third, what should investors expect from us as we continue to integrate the businesses and allocate capital. Let me start with the first question. What is Hornbeck Offshore Services today? The combined Hornbeck is a diversified deepwater offshore services business operating across 3 distinct segments: Marine Transportation & Specialty, Subsea Services and Well Intervention. We're not simply a larger offshore vessel company.

We now have a global reach, especially into additional premier energy basins around the world and participate across a considerably broader portion of the offshore life cycle with an emphasis on traditional and renewable energy and diversity through defense support and emerging technologies. Through our Marine Transportation & Specialty segment, we own and operate supply vessels, flotels and other assets to support drilling, development, military and other specialty activities. In our Subsea Services segment, we own and operate subsea vessels and robotics to provide inspection, repair and maintenance, engineering, construction and specialized project services. And through our Well Intervention segment, we help customers maintain, restore and extend production from existing traditional offshore infrastructure and ultimately provide decommissioning services.

This full life cycle exposure complete with innovative technologies that we deploy is a key part of our investment thesis. Offshore projects create demand for vessels, robotics and Subsea Services. Producing assets require ongoing inspection, repair, maintenance and intervention. And as oil fields mature, customers increasingly need well intervention and ultimately decommissioning services. In addition, our Well Intervention fleet should benefit from higher levels of production enhancement demand and the forecast increases in utilization and day rates for deepwater rigs. With this in mind, I also want to provide an update on our progress towards exiting the activities that are noncore to what I just outlined.

Prior to closing the merger, Helix divested of its shallow water decommissioning business, and we intend to wind down the oil and gas interest, including Thunder Hawk and Droshky that were previously acquired by Helix. We also expect to reduce our reliance on in-chartered vessels over time. We've already replaced one in chartered vessel. Because several existing commitments are long term, that transition will take some time, but the direction is clear. Given the focused portfolio we now operate, our job is to translate this full life cycle platform into higher utilization, stronger margins, greater free cash flow and improved returns on invested capital. Turning now to value creation. We see 4 primary ways that Hornbeck can deliver outsized returns.

First, our diversified platform gives us greater visibility across our customers' offshore programs. That allows us to identify more opportunities, compete for a greater scope of work and deploy a range of integrated assets and services across more projects and geographies. Second, it creates opportunities to improve asset utilization. A MPSV is more valuable when marketed as part of a broader solution, incorporating ROVs, engineering, subsea tooling and/or intervention capabilities. Likewise, our Subsea and Intervention business benefit from access to owned marine assets while creating opportunities for pull-through work for our high-specification OSV fleet. We have positioned the company and its assets into specific markets where we can drive integrated services.

Third, by assembling more capabilities within the same organization, we will retain a greater portion of the revenue, margin and cash flow associated with the projects. And fourth, our scale allows us to eliminate redundant costs and create efficiencies across procurement, maintenance, operations and the supply chain. In terms of what investors should expect from us as we continue to integrate the business and allocate capital, there are a few key points I'd like to highlight. One of the most important opportunities created by the combination is our integrated services. Complex offshore projects frequently require multiple service contractors with different operating schedules and commercial agreements.

The timing and scope of each of those vendors needs to be harmonized and each additional interface creates complexity and increases project risk. By bringing marine assets, ROVs, trenchers, engineering capabilities and intervention systems together under one roof, we can simplify and optimize those interfaces and coordinate a broader scope of work around our customers' requirements. For our customers, this means simpler contracting, more coordinated scheduling and clear accountability for execution. For Hornbeck, it means a greater share of our customer spending, better asset utilization and less economic leakage to third-party providers. We are already seeing the evidence that our customers value this model. This week, we announced service agreements with Shell covering operations in the U.S. Gulf of America.

The contemplated scope brings together assets from all 3 of our operating segments, including a riser-based well intervention vessel, and intervention riser system, ROVs, project management and engineering as well as a high-specification MPSV with ROVs and technical services and a Jones Act-compliant OSV to support these operations. Operations under those agreements are scheduled to commence in 2027 for a 5-year duration for the well intervention vessel and OSV. Importantly, this marks the first 5-year agreement for a Q vessel in over a decade. This is even a broader illustration of the opportunity we saw in combining these 2 companies.

Just like our North Sea award announced in September, these Shell agreements confirm that Hornbeck's unique offering and ability to bundle services is differentiating and positions us for sustainable growth and value creation. We also believe the combined businesses will create additional opportunities to grow our defense support business. We currently have several vessels chartered to the U.S. government performing a variety of work scopes. Most recently, we successfully completed a proof of concept to demonstrate the ability to quickly retrofit autonomous capabilities into a commercial supply vessel that had been previously modified for defense support work scope.

It has been reported that this HOS vessel is the largest vessel retrofitted with autonomy across the entire Department of Defense commercial fleet. Within the full spectrum of our market exposure, we currently see attractive opportunities in both Subsea Services and Well Intervention. In Subsea, one area of particular interest is deep and ultra-deepwater inspection, repair and maintenance. The offshore industry has accumulated a large installed base of subsea infrastructure, and that infrastructure continues to age. At the same time, EPIC or major subsea contractors have accumulated record levels of contracting backlog that will create demand as that backlog moves into execution over the next several years.

Operators need to inspect, repair and maintain these assets, extend their economic lives and support ongoing production. This creates recurring demand for vessels with large subsea cranes, ROVs and specialized technical capabilities, which is where we come in. Our recent organic investment in 8 additional world-class ROV systems is intended to position more of our MPSV fleet to address this opportunity by combining the vessel and subsea capability as these new assets deliver throughout 2027. We also believe Well Intervention gives us exposure to a growing part of the offshore life cycle. As the global offshore infrastructure continues to mature, operators are increasingly focused on maximizing recovery from existing subsea infrastructure they already own.

In many cases, intervention can restore or enhance production without requiring the capital and lead time associated with the new greenfield exploratory development. In addition, attractive commodity prices should drive production enhancement demand and forecasted increases in utilization and rates for deepwater rigs to support offshore drilling campaigns, which should benefit our well intervention fleet. That makes well intervention an important strategic complement to our marine and subsea businesses and gives Hornbeck additional exposure to production and decommissioning customer spending as offshore fields continue to mature. Defense and renewables remain another attractive long-term opportunity. Hornbeck spent the last 25 years developing the U.S.-flagged marine platform, customer relationships and operating capabilities required to serve the defense market.

This, in combination with Helix's subsea robotics, engineering and technical capabilities allows the combined company to now serve a broader range of missions. Our stacked fleet includes 23 Jones Act vessels and 1 Mexican flagged vessel that uniquely afford us the ability to rapidly and efficiently respond to incremental defense requirements. Those vessels can potentially be returned to service more quickly and with less capital than a new build. We will only reactivate capacity when the commercial arrangement appropriately compensates us for the required investment and execution risk. We're also well equipped to support offshore renewable energy projects.

We see indicators that our renewable customers in the North Sea have a growing backlog of projects requiring trenching and ROV services in that region, which is exactly what we're designed to do. I'd also like to touch a little bit on our organic growth strategy, which will remain focused on investments that increase the earnings capability of assets we already own or have under construction. As I mentioned, as a part of our strategy to grow our Subsea Services business, we will be acquiring 8 world-class ROV systems for approximately $56.4 million. Deliveries are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027 and continue throughout the year with 4 systems designated for our 400 class ultra-deepwater newbuilds.

We also expect the first newbuild MPSV to become commercially available late in the third quarter of 2027 and the second in the second quarter of 2028. These highly capable assets designed for demanding subsea work were contemplated from the outset as vessels capable of supporting more technical complex services, including intervention and defense work. As a combined company, our commercial opportunity for these vessels is much broader because now we can market them alongside our robotics, engineering and subsea intervention capabilities. In closing, we believe the long-term deepwater offshore opportunity is especially attractive. But we also know that an attractive market by itself does not guarantee attractive shareholder returns. Performance and execution do.

Our responsibility is to operate safely, maintain asset reliability, price risk appropriately, integrate the business thoughtfully and allocate capital when prospective returns justify the investment. If we execute consistently against those priorities, we believe we can build a company capable of creating value not simply at the top of an offshore cycle, but throughout the cycle. I want to thank all of our offshore and shore-based employees for their continued focus during a period of substantial organizational change. Our team has been working tirelessly to ensure the successful integration of these 2 companies, and I want to recognize their efforts and dedication.

On that note, one thing I want to highlight is that we prioritize share ownership in the new company for our entire shoreside support team, not just the executives. We aim to foster a culture of ownership that is closely aligned with our investors, which we believe makes us unique among our public peers. With that, I'll turn over the call to Potter to take you through the numbers in more detail. Potter?

Robert Adams: Thanks, Todd. Before reviewing our third quarter results, there are 2 important points about this transitional quarter. First, because legacy Hornbeck is the accounting acquirer, our third quarter results include 3 months of legacy Hornbeck, but only 1 month of legacy Helix. Accordingly, the quarter should not be viewed as a run rate quarter for the combined company. Second, the quarter includes $79 million of merger and integration costs and $41 million of accelerated stock-based compensation expense associated with the transaction. With this in mind, our fourth quarter results will be the first to include 3 full months of operations from all 3 segments and will provide a better baseline for sequential comparisons going forward.

Please note, though, that the fourth quarter will reflect normal seasonality, planned dry dock and maintenance activity, project timing, mobilizations and integration costs. Following the merger, we have 326 million total basic shares. Additional details are included in the earnings release and our forthcoming 10-Q. We posted some slides to accompany the earnings release to our website yesterday. In those materials, you will find more information about the merger and certain consolidated and segment financial data, which we have adjusted to reflect results of the combined companies for the third quarter and certain historical periods for illustrative purposes.

With that context, rather than discussing the as-reported results and reviewing variances, which are included in the press release we issued yesterday, I'll walk through the third quarter results on an as-adjusted basis, which reflect the full quarter contribution of both legacy companies. I'll focus on the key financial data provided in the slides and the underlying operating drivers we believe will be most useful in evaluating our performance going forward. Against that backdrop, I'll now provide a recap of our consolidated results. Third quarter revenue was $503 million. Adjusted EBITDA was $155 million or 31% of revenue. Adjusted free cash flow was $99 million, resulting in a free cash flow conversion of 64%.

As we move beyond this transitional quarter, free cash flow conversion will be an important measure of our ability to translate adjusted earnings into capital available for committed investment, balance sheet management and other return-based opportunities. Before returning to the segment results, I wanted to emphasize that these are new reporting segments for the combined company and the historical results of legacy Hornbeck and legacy Helix do not match directly to the new structure. The assets, operations and related results of legacy Hornbeck and legacy Helix have been reassigned among the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments.

Across the 3 segments, we believe the most useful operating statistics for modeling the business moving forward are the number of active vessels, average day rates, utilization and operating expense per vessel day. Together, these measures provide the clearest view of available earnings capacity, pricing, asset productivity and the cost required to generate that revenue. Project and geographic mix will also affect quarterly results, particularly in Subsea Services and Well Intervention. But these core statistics should provide investors with a consistent starting point for evaluating segment margins and cash generation over time. We have included more information, including the vessels that make up each segment in the slides posted to our website yesterday.

Our Marine Transportation and Specialty segment includes the OSVs, flotels and specialty vessels from the legacy Hornbeck fleet. Since this segment only includes legacy Hornbeck vessels, its results reflect a full quarter of operations. Total revenue was $153 million and adjusted EBITDA was $68 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 44%. We operated an average of 38.5 active vessels during the third quarter. Average day rates were approximately $52,000, active utilization was 77% and the resulting effective day rate for the active fleet was approximately $39,900. Subsea Services generated $106 million of revenue and $34 million of adjusted EBITDA, resulting in an adjusted EBITDA margin of 33% for the third quarter.

The active fleet was 12.3 vessels and included the full quarter contribution from 7 legacy Hornbeck vessels and 5 legacy Helix vessels and a partial quarter contribution from 1 vessel. Average day rates were $101,000, utilization was 78% and effective day rates were roughly $78,500. Well Intervention generated $237 million of revenue, $76 million of adjusted EBITDA and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 32%. The average fleet count was 8 for the quarter, inclusive of in-chartered vessels. Utilization was 91% with an average day rate of $349,000 and an effective day rate of $316,000. Please note that the sum of the segments does not reflect the additional results from the unallocated and other segments. Shifting to backlog.

As of September 30th, contracted revenue backlog was approximately $1.9 billion, including approximately $333 million expected during the remainder of 2026, $793 million during 2027 and $741 million thereafter. Our total backlog is comprised of $668 million, $431 million and $760 million for the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments, respectively. While backlog provides meaningful visibility, ultimate realization will depend on project timing, vessel availability and execution. Let me now turn to synergies. At announcement of the merger, we identified at least $75 million of anticipated annual revenue and cost synergies to be realized within the first 3 years after closing, consisting of $45 million of revenue synergies and $30 million of cost synergies.

We have implemented actions representing approximately $20 million of expected annualized cost savings and expect to achieve our targeted cost synergies by the end of the first full year of combined operations. We are also targeting approximately $15 million of revenue synergies within the first year. The recently announced services agreements with Shell demonstrate the commercial opportunities created by the combined platform and the company's ability to provide a broader suite of offshore services to its customers. Beginning with fourth quarter reporting, our goal is to provide clearer visibility into these actions and their effect on margins and free cash flow. Ultimately, the combination should be judged by measurable improvements in earnings, cash conversion and returns.

I will now review some of our key balance sheet and liquidity-related items for the third quarter as well as our capital allocation priorities. We ended the quarter with approximately $472 million of cash, net of $1.6 million of restricted cash. That balance reflects roughly $230 million of payments for deal-related costs, including around $90 million for professional fees and integration, approximately $17 million for the brand licensing agreement and $58 million related to compensation due to the merger triggering a change in control for both legacy companies. We also used approximately $63 million of cash for withholding taxes related to net share settlements due to the vesting of stock previously issued under each legacy company's long-term incentive plan.

Importantly, we funded those obligations with cash rather than using shares, thereby avoiding additional dilution to our shareholders. Total debt had a face value of just over $730 million, and we had no borrowings under our $125 million revolving credit facility. Including revolver capacity, total liquidity was approximately $597 million. This financial flexibility of a healthy cash balance, low financial leverage and ample liquidity is important, and we will remain highly disciplined. Looking ahead, our capital allocation priorities remain straightforward: Maintain safe and reliable operations, fund required maintenance and recertification and complete committed investments that enhance the earnings capability of assets we already own.

Other reactivations, conversions, acquisitions, debt reduction and potential returns of capital will be evaluated based on their potential to create accretive shareholder value. Our 2 U.S.-flagged, Jones Act 400 class MPSVs remain on track for physical shipyard delivery during 2027. We expect approximately $74 million of remaining cash outlays related to the outfitting engineering and post-delivery enhancements, excluding capitalized interest. We expect the first vessel to enter commercial service late in the third quarter of 2027 and the second in 2Q 2028. Separately, we expect the majority of the remaining spending under our approximately $56 million ROV newbuild program to occur in 2027. Turning to the market.

We continue to view the long-term deepwater outlook as constructive, although near-term conditions vary by geography and service line. Activity in the Gulf of America remains measured while we continue to see attractive opportunities across several international markets, including Brazil, the North Sea and Europe. Importantly, the combined company's broader geographic and service line exposure means our investment thesis no longer depends on the activity level of any one single basin. With that context, I'll now spend a few more minutes on our guidance. Based on current backlog, customer commitments and operating plans, we expect adjusted EBITDA of $90 million to $100 million for the fourth quarter of 2026 and $500 million to $550 million for full year 2027.

The fourth quarter range reflects the first full quarter of combined operations, including normal seasonal and operational variability. It should not be annualized from September or viewed as a straight-line progression from the third quarter. Utilization for the fourth quarter is expected to be negatively impacted by 223 days of downtime associated with regulatory dry dockings comprised of 114, 75 and 34 days for the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments, respectively. This compares to 50 days in total for the third quarter of 2026. There are several important assumptions underlying our outlook that I want to make clear about our 2027 guidance.

First, we assume no material earnings contribution from the noncore assets and activities that Todd discussed earlier. Second, 2027 will be a comparatively heavy regulatory dry dock year with scheduled downtime weighted towards the first half. We currently expect 407 days of regulatory dry dock downtime during the first quarter alone, including 148 days in Marine Transportation, 89 days in Subsea Services and 170 days in Well Intervention. When operationally feasible, we intentionally schedule this work during seasonally lower activity periods. Third, the outlook includes the $20 million of cost synergies already implemented and therefore, does not assume realization of the full synergy opportunity.

Fourth, as I just discussed, we assume contribution from the first HOS 400 class MPSV newbuild beginning late in the third quarter 2027. Finally, our guidance assumes U.S. Gulf of America deepwater drilling activity remains consistent with current levels. We are not relying on a material increase in GoA rig activity to achieve the outlook. To the extent customer activity improves from current levels, that could provide additional opportunities, but our base case does not require it. Our 2027 guidance incorporates current expectations for backlog conversion, vessel availability, project timing, geographic and service line mix and normal seasonal variability. We will provide a more detailed 2027 guidance framework when we report our fourth quarter results in February.

Looking ahead, our objective over the coming quarters is to establish a clear combined company baseline and demonstrate measurable progress in our results across margins, free cash flow conversion and synergy realization. These measures connect the strategic case Todd described earlier to the financial outcomes we are accountable for delivering. With that, I'll turn the call back to the operator to entertain questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question we will hear from Keith Beckmann with Pickering Energy Partners.

Keith Beckmann: Obviously, we're a little early in the integration process here, but I just wanted to follow up around, obviously, the Shell contract you guys saw earlier this week, right? But how are you -- just talk a little bit more how you're weaving together kind of the legacy Hornbeck and legacy Helix side of kind of cross-selling and bundling things together a little bit more for us and maybe how that looks going forward as well?

Todd Hornbeck: Yes. Look, it's going great. We just -- it's been 60 days since we announced the merger. The teams are working great. And I think it's a big win to justify why we put these companies together within 60 days, signing a major contract for the company with a Q vessel, a supply vessel and an MPSV and a bundling contract. So I think that's a testament of why we put the companies together. We're getting a tremendous amount of response from our customer base since we announced about these types of opportunities that we can offer today that each individual company could not do on their own before.

So now we can really focus not just on bundling, that's just one aspect, but also life of field services. So we can actually take the entire life of field, use our supply vessels, our MPSVs, robotics, engineering across all of our engineering disciplines, do stimulation work, intervention work and then at the end, the decommissioning and take up all the jewelry and everything on the seaport at a one-stop shop. That's a very unique combination of heavy assets, tooling assets and engineering capability that I think differentiates us from all the other service companies and really puts Hornbeck in a different league of company. We're not just an asset owning company anymore.

We're actually an execution company and integration company as well. So very excited about that. And within 60 days, signing a major contract like that is pretty remarkable.

Keith Beckmann: Awesome. That's very helpful. And then, my second question just kind of revolves around thinking about the Gulf longer term as well. So obviously, the Gulf in the near term here, there's a couple of floaters leaving, it seems. And then -- but maybe how are you guys thinking about that region longer term and a potential return to activity and particularly next year as well on the support vessel side, I mean, what is some of the offsetting factors? Is that some potential defense work? Just maybe how you're thinking about that longer term in the Gulf here.

Todd Hornbeck: Well, the Gulf has been relatively flat on rig count for the last 3 years, but we've expanded our margins and utilization during that time and putting the company together even makes it a more robust company. We're not just a Gulf of Mexico player, even though I believe in long-term basin play, it's a world-class basin for hydrocarbons. I think that will continue in the future. But we operate all over the world. We're a global player now. So -- and with our defense and our alternative opportunities, we can move these assets around very efficiently. And also, we don't really need the rig count to do the bundling and do the life of field services.

And what you've seen also is major announcements with tree installation and development in the Gulf of Mexico that is a big portion of our business with the robotics and the MPSVs and the well intervention and stimulation assets. So I think that combination today, we can still utilize all the PSVs and everything on other projects than just turning a bit. Today, our revenue from direct drilling, whether it's exploratory or development drilling is very small as a percentage of revenue. That is not the story here. It's more the integrated services and all the services geographically we can do.

Operator: And next, we'll move to Don Crist with Johnson Rice.

Donald Crist: Todd, I wanted to expand a little bit on Keith's last question. Specifically on the boat market, the Gulf of America is exceptionally weak at the moment. Are you getting any traction in moving some of your boats, whether it be to West Africa or the Mediterranean through the relationships that Helix had on that side of the business that you may have not had from the Hornbeck side previously?

Todd Hornbeck: Yes, we are. We're getting a tremendous amount of inbounds to look at projects that we didn't have boots on the ground or infrastructure in West Africa and the Med and even the North Sea. So pretty exciting that we have these opportunities that if we so choose, we can move the assets. But what's really coming in is as soon as we announced, our customer base got it. They understood what we were doing. And the influx of us being able to put work packages together to do life of field services and bundling has been more robust than anything else that we've seen.

While we do have a lot of opportunities in the company because of the global reach now, we can do a proper alternative analysis on what's the best -- how we maximize revenue and manage risk because we can weigh all these opportunities against each other for the company. And also what's driving is what you know is our military business, our defense work is really starting to pick up. And you can see just read the papers every day and you know why. But that's a big portion of the company.

And now with the capabilities with ROVs and robotics and some of the tooling that Helix had in its existing fleet and engineering, it opens up a wide array of opportunity for us with our defense work domestically and abroad. So that is another play that's coming very, very strong. So pretty excited about just not only geographic reach, but all of the inbound that we're getting across the globe of looking at projects that we probably never -- individually, we probably wouldn't see if the companies were separated today because of the work packages and the engineering and the back office things that we can do that we couldn't do as each company independent.

Donald Crist: Appreciate that. And one question on the comments on your scripted remarks. I think you said that you wanted to exit charter vessels. Were you referring to the Siem vessels down in Brazil? Or are those vessels that they have not had?

Todd Hornbeck: Well, we look at everything. Everything is on the table. In-chartered vessels, as you know, carry a liability, long-term contracts, and we're a heavy asset-owning company with the soft skills of the engineering and the tooling. So it's better for us to own our own equipment and manage our destiny a little bit better than relying on third parties. Number one, not just to capture the cash flow and the returns, but also when you get to a tight market, if something was to happen to a third-party vessel for any reason at all, it could be pretty difficult to replace. So controlling the destiny of where we're going in the capital return and really lowering the risk.

And look, when you have too many in-chartered vessels, in my mind, it's also a credit issue as well with the rating agencies and others. So we're also looking for the lowest cost of capital for the company over the time period. And we believe that is owning our own equipment and servicing our clients 100%.

Donald Crist: Okay. And just one more final one for me, if I could slip it in. On the M&A front, obviously, you have a really good balance sheet here, which you may have to refinance the debt and put it together here shortly. But after that, are there some attractive targets that may be in a region that you're not operating in today, whether it be Brazil or West Africa or somewhere else that look attractive today?

Todd Hornbeck: There's a tremendous amount of opportunities across the globe to look at. And with our company today, the integration that we've done with the 2 companies, it opens up more opportunities. But as a public company, as investors, natural to ask about our growth plans. The way we think about it is our financial strength provides us significant flexibility to evaluate a wide range of accretive growth opportunities. But always, we're going to focus on increasing shareholder value. So it's got to pass the smell test with us. But I can tell you that there are opportunities around. We just have to weigh that for the risk and the returns versus keeping the capital, returning it back to the shareholders.

Operator: And moving on, we'll hear from James West with Melius Research.

James West: Todd, the Shell transaction or the Shell contract, sorry, is really, really impressive. And I know that Hornbeck has a long legacy relationship with Shell. Curious as to how this came together, the framework? And is this -- what's the applicability of this to other contracts? And has this gotten the notice of other major oil companies?

Todd Hornbeck: Yes, across the board. It is very well noticed. As you can see, and you probably heard from other commentary on other calls, the well intervention and stimulation market is really picking up. A lot of the rigs are going back to on the drill bit. And with the commodity prices where they are and where I think people believe the strip will be forward strip through the next 3 to 5 years, it looks like things are sizing up pretty well. This came together, of course, because Shell noticed that they need a long-term solution for their -- not just their deepwater P&A, but the intervention work and stimulation. And when we announced the companies, it really brought clarity.

They were one of the first to call that said, "Oh my gosh, you can do all of the entire project for us." So that's where the supply boats come in and the MPSVs. And look, we will -- we expect to expand on that relationship. This is just the first phase, but we are getting inbounds from other major oil companies to do the exact same thing. So whether it's a bundling or whether it's life of field services, all of that is coming into focus as a one-stop shop, very easy to contract with us because we own all the equipment.

We can build a lot of efficiencies in with our customers because they're not chartering from 4 or 5 different asset owning companies and trying to marry up the different agreements, the insurances, the time they have to put them on and off. We can streamline that process. We own all the equipment. So we can put it on and off and reduce a tremendous amount of friction cost for them when it's needed and share in some of that savings and that improves our utilization and margins as we build out that franchise, which I think we're probably one of the only ones with the asset collection that we have that can do true cradle-to-grave services with big assets.

So pretty darn excited about it. And I think our customers get it today and good things to come in the future.

James West: And then maybe a quick follow-up for me, maybe unrelated, but on the military business, I know you can't go into a lot of detail here, but it's become a big part of the company. Is there room to grow that further? I mean it's a great kind of consistent cash flow business that underpins your interest expense and things like that. And so curious how you're thinking about that.

Todd Hornbeck: Yes. The way we think about it in the future is that, look, we've got 23 vessels that are able to go quickly to the military at a very low cost. And it's like almost an internal acquisition. It's organic growth, but they've been well maintained. They were the deepwater vessels of the last up cycle. And they are very adaptable to the projects that we're looking at with the military and what we know they need in the future. And as we reported, we've done -- the technology that we're developing with several others on autonomy and AI is really moving that forward.

So yes, there's not just an opportunity just to expand our defense services, but also not just to fees or debt or anything, but actually a profitable -- big profitable segment of the company with a tremendous amount of upside growth there. Look, we're doing a lot with technology. Hornbeck Offshore has always been a technology company first. And what we've done is we developed whether it was back in the day when we were developing the very first DP1 continuous duty rating DP systems or Dynamic Positioning Systems or DP2 or all of the other technology we've brought over the years to the market.

We take that technology and then we just wrap it in a steel hull with different components to do a service. So really, what drives the force of the company and the growth a lot of times is our technology that we're developing right now that we can use on our existing fleet and then eventually ships of the future could be a decade out or for whatever it may be with the military, it may be in alternatives. It may be new ventures in ultra-deepwater complex areas to operate.

So we're pretty excited about the field of view, not just in the oil and gas business, but all the other deepwater regions of the world that have different applications that are coming to the forefront because of technology, and that's where we're at the pointy end of the stick.

Operator: Next from Greg Lewis with BTIG.

Gregory Lewis: Just following up on James' question around the Shell contract. Realizing in the past, Helix used to kind of contract with oil majors for like a minimum amount of utilization on an annual basis. I guess as we look at this multiyear contract, are there minimums of utilization that we should expect? And then are these -- is this kind of -- is this project-based pricing? Or is it more day rate across the different assets that are going to be deployed during the contract?

Todd Hornbeck: Well, look, guys, all of these contracts goes, we're not at liberty to talk about the contract. I mean we put out a press release that Shell has approved. And really, in our next quarter in February, we're going to add that to the backlog. It's not added to the backlog right now, but I can tell you it's substantial and there's growth opportunities there. But yes, the answer, there are minimums with tons of growth opportunities within the minimums. So there is -- it is a major contract for backlog. So that will be included in February when we add it to the backlog. It wasn't included this time.

But for a contract, it is a major piece of business for us that has not just on the face of the contracts that we've already signed, but growth opportunities in other phases as well for other equipment in the company. So this is just the first phase, but this is -- you're on it, on that it is -- it's got minimums with growth opportunities as well. But the minimums are very, very substantial.

Gregory Lewis: And then, Potter, just as we think about the guidance, the $500 million to the $550 million, I don't know what else you -- like as we think about the swing factors in that, just thinking about marine transportation, is that largely the driver between the high end and the low end? And then as we think about utilization, just kind of looking at Slide 17 and looking at the previous, I don't know, last 6 quarters, should we -- is that kind of based on like a high 70% type utilization? Is it mid- high 70s? Is that kind of a fair way to start thinking about '27?

Robert Adams: Yes. I mean we outlined kind of those key assumptions in the prepared remarks, Greg. One of the key things is the heavy dry dock year, and we gave you those numbers in the slide deck and on our guidance slide to show what the impact on utilization should be for those dry dock days. But really, I mean, I think when we think about upside, yes, Marine Transportation, we kind of outlined the Gulf of America, should activity pick up there. We see upside from that basin. But also, as Todd provided, there is a growing Well Intervention market. And with rig utilization tightening and day rates increasing there, that only benefits our assets in that segment.

And then as we build out the IRM business in Subsea, we think that there's additional opportunities there. So as we said, we're constructive on the overall macro. But in the Gulf of America, we're not reliant on increased activity, but that could produce upside to our guidance if that does come to fruition.

Todd Hornbeck: Greg, I would also add to that is that we have a tremendous amount of operating leverage in the business. And not just from -- on every segment, we see growth opportunities, whether the rigs are going back to drilling rigs are doing more exploratory development drilling or the military business with more contracts coming there or even alternatives. But what we've created here is new demand for the company by being able to bundle and do life of field services that didn't exist for each company before. So even without demand drivers increasing, if it stayed flat, we are creating more demand for our equipment by the nature of how we're redoing the business model and the business plan.

We're no longer dependent on just a drilling rig going to work or something that happened with the commodity price going up. We can stay in the environment here and still have a tremendous amount of operating leverage. So with that type of exposure and the strengths of the company that we're putting together, we can really full life cycle exposure that we didn't have before. We've got innovative technologies that we're bringing to create demand as well for our business. The market diversity geographically opening up a tremendous amount of markets. That's opened up demand for the company without changing any of the demand profile out there.

It's opened up demand for us because of putting the companies together, the expanded geographic footprint. But I do believe the share price doesn't fully reflect the value of HOS today. So I think it's a good time to buy. I got to just put that in there.

Todd Hornbeck: Look, I want to thank everybody for joining our call today. We're confident in the value we bring to our customers and our ability to deliver long-term shareholder value. With that, thank you all for joining us, safe sailing, and have a great rest of your day.

#3121. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

#3120. Google Introduces 3 More Top-Level Domain Names, Including .Eat and .Fly

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Prospective website owners can now register domains geared toward food, travel and local bands.

We’re trained to type .com almost on autopilot, but more top-level domains are coming. You’ll soon see websites ending in .eat, .fly and .here. It’s a new way for restaurants, travel agencies and other service providers to customize their online presence.

Google successfully filed these domain types with ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, back in 2012, but only released the new registry options to the public on Tuesday.

There’s always a concern that someone will steal a business’ domain name, a process known as cybersquatting. To prevent new top-level domains from being registered and ransomed at high prices, Google’s partnered registrars offered .eat, .fly and .here websites to registered trademark holders ahead of a wider rollout. This closed access period lasted from Sept. 1 to Nov. 9.

Google’s blog post about the new domains revealed several big businesses that have already secured new web addresses during the trademark holder selloff. Wingstop bought up wingstop.eat, while agriculture and food-tech company Clayton Farms secured the america.eat address. Caddy, Canary and Voltair are some of the businesses with new .fly domains.

The most interesting assortment of companies have tied down .here addresses. In its blog, Google describes .here domains as denoting businesses “where people get things done.” They utilize fairly common words that people might search for. Real-estate app Zillow owns rent.here and sell.here, while bloodtest.here is owned by SiPhox Health, a home blood-testing service.

A number of Google-partnered registrars are now accepting registrations for the three new domain types.

There’s currently a one-time early registration fee associated with registering the new domain names, though it is diminishing and will completely disappear on Nov. 17. After that, any currently unused .eat, .fly and .here names can be registered and maintained at a fixed annual rate, just like any other type of domain.

A representative for Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Unit Conversion is a module to help you skip toggling between the browser and the calculator. Pixel 6 and above phones are also getting Live Location Sharing for Pixel VIPs.

Finally, Pixel 10 phones are getting Extreme Charging Mode that quickly charges your phones to full.

Your Pixel Watch isn't getting as many features as the phones, but the big one is "Step-by-Step Workouts." Basically, your watch will give you step-by-step instructions for each exercise in your routine. It will also log reps, weights and track metrics from your Watch, or your phone.

Google announced that Create My Widgets, Gemini call Screen and Notification Summaries, outlined above, are "coming soon"; no specific date was provided.

Phone to Watch Unlock is also coming soon to Pixel Watch 3 and new models. This feature will let you unlock your watch with a nearby paired phone. No date was provided here either.

#3118. Reddit launches AI-powered Reviews feature – with 10,000 products to start

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Reddit is adding AI-generated product reviews that compile real user sentiment from across communities. Here's how they work.

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit announced a new feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit says you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that says, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative said they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it says, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”

You’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a big plus.

#3117. Half of New Games on Steam Are Now Made With AI. How Does This Reflect the Gaming Industry?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of those games are unpopular, with 10 or fewer reviews from gamers.

Steam, the digital marketplace for PC games from game studio Valve, has hit a major milestone, sparking pushback from parts of the gaming community: Approximately 50% of new Steam games in October were made with the help of AI.

This underscores a growing trend in gaming, where more games are made with some form of AI assistance — specifically, generative AI, which developers have used to generate code, art assets, voice lines and more. Developers are adopting the technology in increasing numbers.

The numbers come from a Reddit user who goes by Ploz, and who used Steam’s publicly available data to see how many newly released games relied on AI in some capacity. This was possible because of Valve’s AI disclosure policy for newly released games, which requires developers to state whether they used AI in making their game. The disclosure is part of the storefront’s publicly accessible records, allowing anyone to view it.

A Valve representative did not respond to a request for comment.

The data is a snapshot of the tidal wave of AI-made games flooding storefronts, most prominently Steam. But crucially, Valve has chosen not to limit this flood, washing its hands of the problem and leaving gamers to fend for themselves in finding quality games. Developers had already been struggling to get their games noticed, and Valve’s limited curation seems completely unprepared for the firehose of AI-made games churned out on an increasing scale.

Valve implemented the AI disclosure policy in January 2024 to increase developer transparency. At the time, only 1.4% of newly released games used AI. This increased to 13.4% by the end of 2024, then to 24% by the end of 2025. It now sits at 49.9%.

There are some caveats. The AI disclosure is only required for games that use AI to create player-facing content, such as artwork, sound, character dialogue and localization. The 49.9% figure is specific to these types of games and doesn’t account for developers who use AI for behind-the-scenes tasks such as coding and bug fixes. A Google Cloud survey conducted in August 2025 showed that 87% of developers use AI for backend work, which doesn’t require disclosure on Steam.

So it’s likely that the number of games on Steam built with AI assistance is greater than 50%. Ploz notes that the only way users can avoid AI-generated games is to manually check for AI disclosures.

According to Ploz, the most common use of AI in game development is for artwork, which was mentioned in 63% of disclosures. Text and translations gobbled up 30%, while music (21%), code (16%) and voices (7%) rounded out the list. Many developers had more than one of those areas named in their disclosure, and about a quarter of developers said they were using AI for their Steam store pages and marketing.

About 3% of developers used AI directly as a game mechanic. One such example is a driving simulator called Teach My Little Sister How to Drive. Developers use AI in the game to interpret a player’s voice commands and generate the sister’s responses. To keep a playable demo of the game available to the public, the development team, Easy Fox, is paying $1,000 every day just to cover these AI operating costs — an expense so high that it was forced to take out a loan simply to keep the demo running.

For development, there are loads of options. The Unity 6 engine came out in October 2024 and includes AI code assistance, AI asset generation and third-party integration with Claude Code, Gemini and Grok. Anthropic’s Claude is a fairly popular option among smaller developers, since it supports the ability to vibe code whole games, with ChatGPT, Gemini and GitHub Copilot as other options.

Many of the games being released with the AI disclosure on Steam can be classified as slop — a derogatory term gamers have applied liberally to titles that heavily lean on generative AI for development and look derivative of other popular games. According to Ploz, most AI-enabled games are small: Around 47% of new games with fewer than 10 reviews have an AI disclosure. Among developers who released more than 10 games in a year, 68% of those games included the disclosure.

Games with AI disclosures received fewer positive reviews on average than those without. And among all newly released games with more than 1,000 reviews, only 17% include an AI disclosure. That means gamers are still gravitating toward games without an AI disclosure and pushing back against games that use the technology.

Developers seem aware of this. CNET reached out to two dozen well-known developers, including Epic Games, EA, Activision Blizzard, Ubisoft, PlayStation Studios and many others. All of them declined to comment.

Bigger studios may be using AI in their development, but it’s hard to tell the scale. There’s no such thing as an AI audit yet, and the industry seems to be relying on voluntary disclosure for now. Steam’s disclosure policy has outed smaller developers who are either worried about violating the policy and being taken off the digital storefront, or aren’t worried about the negative effects of disclosure.

A lot of dominoes had to fall for this to happen. The availability of AI tools and the increasing ease of use are definite contributors. Subreddits like r/AIGameDev have plenty of examples of people putting together games with just a few days or weeks of vibe coding, which is a lot shorter than the standard video game development cycle, which can stretch over years depending on the scale, production level and graphics quality. This practice has exploded over the last couple of years, resulting in a lot of games getting launched that are made mostly or entirely with AI.

Many of these games end up on Steam, which doesn’t have a policy limiting AI-developed games.

“Digital storefronts like Steam have already struggled to moderate low-effort and poor-quality games, as well as copycats stealing other games’ ideas,” said CNET Managing Editor David Lumb.

Valve openly admits its role in this, stating that the problem definitely exists but that the company doesn’t “want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

It takes a similar stance on AI cloning, with Valve’s Tom Giardino telling developers that “you must continue to grow your game by adding features, personality and creativity that stem from your own perspective as a developer.”

These policies essentially allow any AI-developed game or clone to reach the Valve storefront without pushback, which certainly contributes to the flood of newly released games with some form of player-facing AI involvement in their development.

Rival store Epic Games has a similar stance, allowing basically any game that wants to be there. The company declined to comment further about this, but CEO Tom Sweeney is an avid supporter of AI in video game development, stating that it was “perfectly logical” for developers to rely on AI to handle the mundane grunt work that takes up most of a developer’s time.

While Steam and Epic Games tend to take a more lax attitude toward AI slop, other storefronts like Itch.io are not. Itch.io has a whole policy against AI slop and the company has willingly, and at times gleefully, deleted terabytes of AI slop from its storefront. It also requires developers to disclose if they used AI but takes a much more consumer-friendly approach by letting users filter those out of search results if they don’t want to see them.

Some measures are being taken to address the proliferation of AI slop, but none will entirely stop the problem. Cloning has been a problem for many years. Mobile gamers of a certain vintage may remember the flock of Flappy Bird clones that appeared on app stores after the original game went down, and those weren’t even made with AI.

AI makes cloning much easier and faster, and some AI companies are addressing it. Anthropic recently changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games. Anthropic engineering leader Addy Osmani posted on X that using Claude to copy games infringes on intellectual property rights and violates Anthropic’s policy.

However, during CNET’s testing, we found we could still make games resembling popular titles, so cloning remains possible with a little creativity.

“This has come up over and over on the subreddit r/GameDev, and there’s no real solution if Steam and other digital storefronts don’t stem the flood of low-quality AI games drowning out the labors of love that entertain and innovate,” Lumb said.

Many developers openly oppose AI and refuse to use it in their own work. However, as the Steam stats show, that crowd’s output appears to be getting smaller and smaller every year amid the unending stream of AI games.

#3116. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."
