#3014. Tech Sell-Off: 3 Stocks Most Vulnerable and 3 Built to Hold Up

The line between the stocks in trouble and the ones holding up may come down to one question: Who is paying for the data centers?

The Nasdaq Composite index has taken a beating over the past month, falling roughly 8.5% from its Oct. 6 record even after Monday's rebound. And some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI) have suffered considerably larger losses.

Investors have plenty to worry about. Questions about AI spending, higher interest rates, rising oil prices tied to the Iran war, and the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections have all contributed to the sell-off.

But not every beaten-down technology stock faces the same risks. Some companies have serious financial challenges that could become more difficult in this environment. Others have the earnings, competitive advantages, and financial resources to weather the downturn.

Here are three stocks that look particularly vulnerable, followed by three that appear better equipped to hold up.

Nebius Group (NBIS -5.27%) has been one of the biggest casualties of the tech sell-off, with its shares falling 35.6% over the past 30 days.

The company is building AI infrastructure and renting out computing capacity to customers, putting it at the center of the enormous spending boom. But building data centers requires substantial up-front investments, and Nebius doesn't have the established earnings base of larger technology companies.

That creates a problem for investors concerned about returns on AI infrastructure investments. Nebius needs to keep expanding capacity to meet demand, but financing that expansion becomes more difficult when borrowing costs rise, and investors become less willing to fund aggressive growth.

Its business also faces potential regulatory complications following the midterm elections, particularly if governments impose new restrictions on data center development.

Nebius has substantial growth opportunities, but its capital requirements make it particularly exposed to a prolonged downturn.

Intel (INTC -2.09%) is in even worse shape than Nebius right now, as the stock is down 44.6% over the past month.

Intel has been spending heavily to rebuild its manufacturing capabilities while competing with Advanced Micro Devices in processors and trying to establish itself as a major contract chip manufacturer. That's an expensive strategy, particularly when its core business is struggling.

The company's disappointing fourth-quarter outlook sent shares plunging 28.6% on Oct. 30 -- the stock's worst one-day performance since 1974.

Intel needs more demand and improved profitability to justify its investment plans. Higher interest rates and investors' growing reluctance to fund expensive technology projects only complicate that effort.

Oracle (ORCL -1.51%) is down 11.8% over the past month, a relatively modest loss compared with Nebius and Intel. But its exposure to the AI infrastructure spending boom deserves attention.

Oracle is spending heavily to expand its cloud infrastructure business, including data centers designed to support AI workloads. That could generate significant revenue over time, but the up-front investment weighs on Oracle stock.

The company's growing reliance on debt financing adds another complication. Higher interest rates make financing more expensive, while concerns about the profitability of AI infrastructure projects could pressure Oracle's valuation.

Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) has fallen 22.5% over the past month, but the sell-off hasn't changed its position as the dominant supplier of AI accelerators.

The distinction matters because Nvidia sells the chips that power the data centers companies such as Oracle and Nebius are building. It doesn't have to finance those facilities itself.

Nvidia also benefits from its CUDA software platform, which makes it difficult for customers to switch to competing hardware without additional development work.

But there's a more immediate problem. The company's board announced on Sunday that it has opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a business executive allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence. Huang has acknowledged the relationship and apologized to his wife and family, but the issue raises questions about the company and sent the stock price down on Monday.

I think the issue is unfortunate and a distraction, but I don't see it changing the long-term narrative around Nvidia and its role as the leading supplier of AI processors.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.23%) stock dipped 14.8% over the last month, despite the company reporting outstanding third-quarter results. Revenue was up 96% from a year ago, and U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148%. The company's rapid growth in bringing on new commercial customers suggests that businesses are finding practical uses for AI rather than merely experimenting with the technology.

Here's the other thing I really like about Palantir: Its software business doesn't require building enormous data centers to generate additional revenue.

The biggest concern is valuation. Palantir has commanded a premium stock price, and its forward price-to-sales ratio remains close to 50. Even outstanding earnings growth doesn't guarantee investors will continue to pay such a high multiple.

Micron Technology (MU -1.10%) stock has fallen 29.3% over the past month, making it one of the hardest-hit semiconductor stocks.

Micron makes high bandwidth memory (HBM) essential for AI accelerators, as well as DRAM and NAND memory that is used throughout the technology industry. Its latest quarterly results demonstrated how dramatically AI demand has improved its business.

For its fiscal fourth quarter, ended Sept. 3, Micron's revenue was $54.23 billion, a huge increase from $11.32 billion a year ago. Its operating cash flow was $43.97 billion.

Today's AI infrastructure requires increasing amounts of memory, particularly HBM. Micron is selling a critical component rather than betting primarily on the future profitability of data centers. That gives it a stronger position than companies whose expansion depends heavily on outside financing.

#3013. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

#3012. Celestica: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Custom AI chip platforms are becoming a major revenue driver for Celestica as hyperscalers shift toward proprietary processors.

In its third-quarter 2026 financial results and investor day call, held on Oct. 27, 2026, Celestica (CLS +0.43%) announced that full-year 2027 revenue is projected to reach $40 billion behind accelerating demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The enterprise hardware manufacturer is rapidly expanding production capacity and working capital investments to meet multiyear commitments from major technology customers. Three key takeaways from the presentation outline how the company is positioning itself for sustained growth.

Demand for high-speed network switches in data centers is shifting rapidly toward faster transmission speeds. Management projects 1.6T (terabit per second) networking equipment will generate more revenue than 800G units in 2027 as hyperscale cloud providers upgrade their infrastructure.

Tech leaders are moving beyond off-the-shelf graphics processors toward application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), custom microchips engineered for specialized artificial intelligence workloads. Celestica is building hardware for major custom chip programs, including Google's tensor processing unit (TPU) platform and OpenAI's Jalapeño architecture.

To support $20 billion of expected top-line growth in 2027, the company plans capital expenditures (spending on physical assets and manufacturing facilities) of $1.5 billion to $2 billion. Management is deploying working capital and expanding facilities in Texas, Thailand, and Mexico to handle massive product rollouts.

Data center capacity constraints are extending customer commitments further into the future, creating multiyear visibility for hardware providers. Customers are engaging in long-term capacity planning to secure necessary manufacturing space and power availability.

Structural advantages in joint design, automated assembly, and liquid cooling position the business to capture long-term market share. Management is watching working capital efficiency, supply chain lead times, and factory utilization as capacity expands globally.

#3009. Lightwave Logic (LWLG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Foundry delays push volume production to 2028 despite a Foxconn milestone.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lightwave Logic, Inc. (LWLG -10.59%) reported a revised timeline for volume production while achieving system-level validation of its technology through a demonstration with Foxconn. Management indicated that the transition from initial demonstrations to commercial scaling is currently influenced by extended foundry production cycles and process qualification requirements. The company is focusing its resources on enabling its ecosystem of five major customers and four foundry partners to integrate electro-optic polymers into silicon photonics platforms for artificial intelligence infrastructure. Financial priorities remain centered on maintaining liquidity through the development phase as the company prepares its Denver facility and negotiates manufacturing partnerships for higher-volume requirements.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Lightwave Logic's Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Business Update. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Nick Teves. Please go ahead.

Nick Teves: Thank you, operator, and good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for joining us today for Lightwave Logic's Third Quarter Financial Results and Business Update Call. I'm joined on today's call by Lightwave Logic's President and Chief Executive Officer, Yves LeMaitre; and Lightwave Logic's Chief Financial Officer, Fred Graffam. [Operator Instructions] A replay will be posted to the company's website shortly after the call concludes. Some of the matters we'll discuss on this call, including statements and our business outlook, are forward-looking, and as such, this call speaks only as of today, November 10, 2026. Such statements may be considered forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

The matters discussed on this call are subject to known and unknown risks and uncertainties, and these risks and uncertainties can cause actual operating results to differ materially from those expressed in the call. A more detailed description of the risks our company faces is more fully described by the company under the caption Risk Factors included in the most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q. As always, Lightwave Logic assumes no obligation to update the information presented on this conference call. Lastly, you are cautioned that any time-sensitive information may no longer be accurate at the time of replay, listening or transcript reading. With that, I'll turn the call over to Yves.

Yves LeMaitre: Thank you, Nick, and good afternoon, everyone. Before turning to our quarterly progress, I want to put our work at Lightwave Logic in the context of a broader industry shift. One of the main themes of our previous calls has been the convergence of photonics and semiconductors, and recent developments show that convergence is accelerating. As AI systems grow, their performance increasingly depends on the ability to move data through optical connections with greater bandwidth, lower power consumption and a smaller footprint. This is bringing photonic materials closer to the heart of semiconductor design, enabling new architecture for scale-out and scale-up connectivity among AI accelerators, processors and switches.

Future scaling architectures will bring optical connectivity even closer to the compute, requiring tighter integration of photonic materials and advanced packaging technologies. Leading semiconductor design and manufacturing companies are incorporating optical technologies and materials into their road maps. Marvell's recently announced agreement to acquire Lumentum underscores this direction with plans to bring semiconductor and optical capabilities under one roof to address these emerging requirements. Our recently announced collaboration with Hon Hai Technology Group, otherwise known as Foxconn, incorporating our electro-optic polymers into a scale-out optical transceiver is a concrete example of our role in this transition.

Foxconn plays a critical role in the semiconductor ecosystem by integrating advanced chips into complex electronic systems and providing the manufacturing scale to bring those systems into high-volume production. We believe this industry shift creates a compelling opportunity for Lightwave Logic. Our proprietary materials combine high-speed performance and power efficiency with compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing processes, positioning us to help customers integrate advanced optical capabilities into silicon photonics platforms. During the third quarter, we continued to make progress advancing Lightwave Logic's electro-optic polymer technology towards commercial qualification and ultimately volume production.

Our efforts remain focused on working closely with customers and foundry partners to establish the technical performance, reliability and manufacturing processes necessary to bring our technology into commercial products. In October, we achieved an important system-level validation milestone through the public demonstration of our technology within an optical transceiver developed by Foxconn, and I will cover this project in more detail during this call. On the manufacturing side, we continue to invest and expand our Perkinamine production infrastructure in Denver, Colorado. To ramp capacity of our back-end of line process, we are in advanced negotiation with a leading specialist in wafer-level optical manufacturing whose material processing and encapsulation capabilities can help scale silicon organic hybrid solutions for AI.

I'll discuss these developments today, along with our updated expectations for the timing of volume production and the priorities guiding our efforts as we move closer to 2027. So let me begin with customers. On October 29, we announced that Foxconn will demonstrate an optical transceiver, incorporating a silicon organic hybrid optical engine enabled by Lightwave Logic's electro-optic polymer technology. The demonstration at Hon Hai Tech Day in Taipei marked an important milestone for Lightwave Logic and meaningful validation of our progress with Foxconn. What makes this demonstration significant is that it goes beyond the performance of individual materials or devices.

It shows our technology operating within a functional optical engine and transceiver designed to address the high-speed, low-power requirements of next-generation AI networks. It provides tangible system-level evidence of how our polymer platform can be incorporated into customer products, and I want to recognize the teams whose collaborative efforts made this milestone possible. This project illustrates the work that takes place during Stage 3 of our design win process. We began working with Foxconn in the first half of 2025 and have now demonstrated the first iteration of an optical engine capable of supporting 200 gigabits per second per lane. We also want to be clear about what this milestone means.

A functioning transceiver demonstration is an important step towards product qualification. Further chip design iterations, integration, reliability testing, manufacturing preparation and customer-specific qualification activities are required before a program can move into volume production or Stage 4 of our design win process. We consider Stage 4 reached when our customers' product is fully qualified, accepted by the end user and ready to be manufactured and shipped in volume with consistently high yields. Every Stage 3 program must progress through a rigorous development and qualification process. Let me explain that in more detail because it is a recurring question from shareholders.

The sequence varies by customer and application, but typically begins with alpha devices or early optical engine prototypes integrated into test platforms or evaluation boards. The next step is to design and produce beta devices that meet the target specification for integration into the customer's transceiver. Once the silicon photonics chips have been fabricated and the necessary back-end processing completed, testing takes place at both the chip and assembled transceiver levels. This covers optical and electrical performance, mechanical and thermal requirements and other application-specific criteria. At the transceiver level, it also includes software functionality wherever applicable. Comprehensive reliability testing will also be completed on both the photonic chip and the finished product.

This design and qualification process assumes that in the background, the silicon foundries have qualified their own equipment and processes and have achieved predictable yields. This is usually announced to the external customers with a new PDK release, including the steps necessary to produce SOH modulators. In parallel, our customers' new product introduction or NPI teams prepare the optical engine and transceiver manufacturing line for volume production. Equipment must be installed and qualified operators trained and assembly processes and test systems validated to achieve the required throughput, consistency and yields. The final critical step is end user qualification.

Sample products are delivered to the end user, which may be a hyperscaler or an AI infrastructure supplier for testing within its own systems. Those customers must confirm compatibility, performance and reliability in their intended operating environment. Once these requirements and the manufacturing readiness criteria have been met, the product can move into commercial volume shipments. In addition to Foxconn and Marvell, which we have previously disclosed, we have 3 other Fortune Global 500 customers in Stage 3. Each program is progressing through its own development and qualification requirements, and our team is focused on helping these customers advance towards Stage 4.

Ultimately, Stage 4 is where the necessary technical and qualification criteria have been satisfied, commercial terms have been agreed upon and programs can move towards volume production. Now let me turn to our silicon photonics foundry activities. On our second quarter call, we reported 3 dedicated foundry runs underway with 2 wafer sets expected in August and a third foundry expected to deliver wafers in the fourth quarter and a dedicated run with our fourth partner progressing towards tape-out. As a reminder, our active foundry ecosystem includes GlobalFoundries, Tower Semiconductor, SilTerra and the fourth partner that remains unnamed. I'm pleased to report that we received wafers from 2 of our foundry partners during the third quarter.

Following receipt, our engineering teams performed the necessary back-end processing, including depositing and poling our electro-optic polymer encapsulating the devices, preparing them for testing and completing characterization. Chips received on an expedited schedule from one of our foundry partners showed promising results and were used in the transceiver demonstration at Hon Hai Tech Day. We expect to receive additional wafers from that foundry by the end of 2026. Our customer currently plans to launch another run in early 2027, targeting the final product configuration. Our second foundry partner ran into process issues at one of their facilities, which translated into a limited number of usable chips.

This foundry partner is expected to deliver 2 new sets of high-performance chips from 2 different manufacturing locations during the first half of 2027. We expect wafers from our third foundry partner in December 2026, while the wafer run with our fourth foundry partner is tentatively scheduled for the first half of 2027. These programs are progressing against a backdrop of strong demand and significant pressure on the optical supply chain. Shortages of indium phosphide lasers, particularly electro-absorption modulated lasers, or EMLs, are accelerating interest in silicon photonics architectures that use continuous wave, or CW lasers. CW lasers are simpler devices than EMLs, easier to produce, and these architectures typically use fewer lasers.

We believe this shift towards silicon photonics further validates the opportunity for electro-optic polymers, which can be integrated into silicon photonics to provide higher performance modulation. At the same time, this demand creates near-term challenges for silicon photonics foundries. Our foundry partners are prioritizing the immediate need for additional silicon photonics production capacity, which can affect the resources and schedules available to qualify new materials and processes. They are also managing the need for additional capacity investment and expansion. These pressures have extended our development time lines and continue to affect our schedule. We remain closely engaged with each partner to advance our programs and appreciate their support under these demanding conditions.

The value of this work extends beyond individual foundry runs. Each completed run provides information that helps us refine the device performance, improve manufacturing yield and achieve greater consistency in subsequent runs. We also incorporate these findings into our process design kit, or PDK, to support future customer designs and foundry integrations. Although our foundry programs are at different stages of maturity, progress across this ecosystem continues to strengthen the manufacturing foundation needed to scale our technology. I also want to address what these time lines mean for our expectations for volume production. On our second quarter call, we discussed the goal of beginning volume production in the second half of 2027.

We now expect volume production to begin in 2028, reflecting longer foundry wafer production schedules and process qualification cycles alongside the remaining customer development and product qualification work. Throughout 2027, our focus will be on completing these activities and helping our customers advance towards Stage 4. We will continue to report meaningful technical, manufacturing and commercial milestones as they are achieved. With that, I will turn the call over to Fred to review our third quarter financial results and financial priorities.

Fred Graffam: Thank you, Yves, and good afternoon, everyone. Since joining Lightwave Logic, my focus has been on supporting disciplined execution as the company advances its customer programs, foundry work and manufacturing readiness. During the third quarter, our investment priorities remained centered on advancing our technology and preparing the organization to support commercialization and production at scale. We continue to evaluate these investments against the technical and commercial milestones they are intended to support with a focus on maintaining appropriate liquidity and aligning our spending with the progression of customer programs. Turning to the financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Net sales were approximately $38,000 compared with approximately $29,000 in the prior year period.

Revenue remains limited at this stage and will be driven principally by the achievement of technical and commercial milestones in existing development contracts. As of September 30, 2026, the company had approximately $100,000 of deferred revenue, which is expected to be recognized upon the achievement of these milestones. Net loss was approximately $7.2 million or $0.05 per share compared with approximately $5.1 million or $0.04 per share in the prior year period. The increase in net loss is principally due to year-over-year increase in operating expenses, reflecting continued investments in electro-optic polymer development and production, device performance and reliability, foundry integration and prototype development and testing.

We also continue to invest in intellectual property and customer engagement as well as the people, systems and infrastructure required to support commercialization. During the quarter, we made targeted hires across key engineering, manufacturing and commercial functions, along with continued improvement in our IT infrastructure, financial and operational systems, reporting and cost controls. Our objective is to build the capabilities needed to support multiple customer programs and future production requirements while maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation. For the quarter, research and development expense was approximately $4.3 million compared with approximately $2.9 million in the prior year period. General and administrative expense for the quarter was approximately $3.7 million compared with approximately $2.3 million in the prior year period.

Turning to our balance sheet. As of September 30, 2026, we held approximately $87.8 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities compared with approximately $95.9 million at June 30, 2026. Our balance sheet continues to provide significant financial flexibility to execute our strategic priorities, and we believe we have sufficient liquidity to fund our operating plan into 2028. Cash used in operating activities was approximately $15 million for the first 9 months of 2026 compared with approximately $10.4 million in the first 9 months of 2025, including approximately $5.2 million during the third quarter of 2026.

Purchases of property and equipment were approximately $2.9 million for the first 9 months of 2026 compared with approximately $1 million in the prior year period. These investments support our continued technology development and production readiness, including laboratory and manufacturing equipment, clean room and quality control capabilities and the infrastructure necessary to support customer programs as they advance. We continue to manage liquidity closely against our progress towards commercialization, including the results of our technical work, customer qualification, manufacturing readiness and advancement of commercial arrangements. As these programs progress, our approach is to build the necessary manufacturing supply chain and operating capabilities in step with verified customer requirements.

In summary, we remain focused on aligning our investments with the company's commercialization priorities and long-term value creation strategy. We believe our financial position and operational investments provide a solid foundation to execute our current organic commercialization plan, support continued research and development and prepare the organization for future growth and production at scale. With that, I will turn the call back to Nick for Q&A.

Nick Teves: Thank you, Fred. We received a number of questions from investors in advance of today's call. We've consolidated those submissions around the topics raised most frequently, and we'll now address several of those questions. Our first question is, on the second quarter call, management discussed beginning volume production in the second half of 2027. What specifically has changed in your assessment of the commercialization time line? And what key technical manufacturing and customer qualification milestones should investors expect during 2027 as you work toward volume production in 2028?

Yves LeMaitre: The main challenge we have been facing in 2026 is a slower pace of silicon photonics foundries, both in terms of production cycles and PDK process qualification. So today, this is our main hurdle to speed up the introduction of silicon organic hybrid modulators incorporating our materials. Obviously, together with our customers, we also have to execute flawlessly all of the design and qualification activities I described earlier. At this time, our engineering team is 100% focused on accelerating the enablement of our silicon foundry partners, both for front-end and back-end, as well as supporting the transition to commercial revenue of our 5 lead customers.

Regarding the production of our Perkinamine in our Denver facility, I'm pleased with the progress we have made over the last few quarters.

Nick Teves: With the pressure on AI infrastructure stocks and questions on CapEx funding, is your revised timing for production volume tied to a slowdown in R&D investment for next-gen 400G solutions?

Yves LeMaitre: No, not at all. All of our programs continue with the same intensity and our customers continue to invest into a path towards 400G per lane in all types of applications from scale-across to scale-up and potentially scaling in the future. We are also seeing an increase in activities beyond 400G per lane, especially in the field of POH or plasmonic organic hybrid solution.

Nick Teves: What were the principal findings from recent foundry wafer testing and characterization, particularly regarding device performance, repeatability and manufacturing yield? Beyond the foundry runs themselves, what additional progress is needed to scale the back-end processing and manufacturing capabilities required for commercial production?

Yves LeMaitre: That is a good question. On the back end of line for polymer processing onto the silicon photonics chip, this is a big area of focus with our customers on reaching wafer scale back end of line with a path towards both high volume and larger 300-millimeter wafers. As you know, this activity currently resides in Denver, but our plan is to outsource it to a partner specializing in wafer testing and material processing. As I mentioned earlier, we are actively negotiating an agreement with that company and kicked off the technical project a few months ago.

Nick Teves: What is the status of the second material supply and licensing agreement previously discussed by management? And are there specific technical qualification or commercial milestones that must be achieved before an agreement can be finalized?

Fred Graffam: Yes. Thanks for the question. On the second material supply and licensing agreement, all I can say at this time is that it's an ongoing and active negotiation. This is obviously a sensitive and confidential matter protected by nondisclosure agreements. And unfortunately, I'm not in a position to share more at this time.

Nick Teves: With volume production now expected to commence in 2028, how does the revised time line affect the company's anticipated investment requirements and capital allocation priorities? And how does the current liquidity position support the commercialization plan?

Fred Graffam: As I noted previously, our liquidity position provides significant financial flexibility with sufficient cash to execute our business plan into 2028. Importantly, the revised timing for volume production does not fundamentally change how we think about capital allocation. We will continue to actively manage our liquidity to ensure that we have the resources necessary to support our customers and execute our commercialization plan while remaining disciplined about the timing of our investments. In particular, we will ensure that the timing and level of our investments will be aligned with the expected business requirements and the benefits we expect those investments to generate.

Nick Teves: Are both 200G per lane and 400G per lane solutions active development priorities? And what additional work is required to commercialize 400G per lane?

Yves LeMaitre: Yes, both are active development priorities. We view 200G per lane as a stepping stone for 400G per lane with most of the technical activities overlapping. Obviously, 400G per lane requires more demanding performance specifications, particularly in terms of bandwidth, but the programs are very similar. What is different is what happens beyond 400G per lane. This is where new solutions might be required beyond SOH and where plasmonics might play an important role. Our CTO and advanced technology group is leading these activities.

Nick Teves: Thank you, Yves and Fred, and thank you to everyone who submitted questions. We appreciate your continued interest and engagement. A replay of today's call will be available in the Events and Presentations section of the company's Investor Relations website. Operator, this concludes today's conference call.

#3005. Resideo (REZI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Branded growth and cost discipline kept margins climbing for 14 quarters.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Resideo Technologies, Inc. (REZI -2.99%) completed its transition to a stand-alone building technologies company following the official spin-off of its distribution business. Management reported that total revenue growth was driven by volume and pricing power across core sales channels despite a challenging housing market. The company is shifting its strategic focus away from lower-margin outside design manufacturing and toward its own branded security and comfort products. Operational initiatives, including manufacturing site consolidations and SKU rationalization, are intended to reduce the cost structure and improve utilization across the global footprint.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Resideo Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Chris Lee, Global Head of Strategic Finance. Please go ahead.

Christopher Lee: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us for Resideo's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me on today's call is Tom Surran, Resideo's Chief Executive Officer; and Shane Harrison, Resideo's Chief Financial Officer. This afternoon's call contains forward-looking statements. Statements other than historical facts made during this call may constitute forward-looking statements and are not guarantees of future performance or results and involve a number of risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements as a result of a number of factors, including those described from time to time in Resideo's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company assumes no obligation to update any such forward-looking statements.

We identify the principal risks and uncertainties that affect our performance in our annual report on Form 10-K and other SEC filings. In addition, we will discuss non-GAAP and stand-alone supplemental financial measures on today's call. These financial measures, which can sometimes be identified by the use of adjusted or stand-alone in the description of the measure should be considered in addition to, not as a substitute for or in isolation from our GAAP results. Stand-alone measures are supplemental financial measures intended to provide historical results before the ADI spin-off on a more comparable basis to the company following the spin-off.

Reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP and stand-alone financial measures are included in our earnings release as well as our financial data workbook, which are accessible on the Investor Relations page of our website at investor.resideo.com. Unless stated otherwise, all numbers and results discussed on today's call other than revenue and gross margin are on a non-GAAP or stand-alone basis. We completed the spin-off of ADI on August 3, and the financial statements presented in our third quarter 2026 earnings release, earnings call and Form 10-Q filing reflect the continuing operations of Resideo and the treatment of ADI as a discontinued operation for all periods presented.

Recast income statements reconciling historical Resideo results to Resideo GAAP results from continuing operations for each quarter of 2025 and 2026 have been provided in our earnings release and our financial data workbook. With that, I will turn the call over to Tom.

Thomas Surran: Thank you, Chris, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. In our first quarter following the spin-off of ADI, Resideo delivered both top and bottom line third quarter results that were near the high end of our outlook. This is a testament to the team's continued resilience, strong execution and commitment to delivering what we promised at our recent Investor Day. Total revenue was driven by both volume growth and pricing across most of our sales channels. Our gross margin was 40.4% as customers continue to see the value of our differentiated nondiscretionary products. We accomplished this in a challenging housing environment.

Stand-alone adjusted EBITDA was $154 million, growing 5% year-over-year as our teams demonstrated cost discipline that helped drive operating leverage in the business. Professional installers are adopting the differentiated products we design and manufacture, resulting in Resideo winning business. Leveraging our scale and experience enables us to navigate through the inflationary cost environment while also creating opportunities to invest in our future growth. Our execution is rooted in a mindset of continuous improvement in all that we do, and we believe that mindset will be the driving force for Resideo's continued success. Let's walk through the dynamics for revenue growth in the quarter.

In the third quarter, we reported total revenue of $727 million, growing 3% year-over-year, which includes an unfavorable impact of approximately 50 basis points from foreign currency exchange. Let me unpack the growth rate further. We achieved 6% or $41 million of growth across all sales channels, excluding OEM security. We consider these non-OEM security sales channels to be our core because they are the foundation that underlie our future growth and earnings potential. Let's walk through the key drivers for each of our core sales channels. Performance in the retail channel was exceptional, with revenue growth of 15% year-over-year, driven by both volume and pricing power.

Volumes were robust for our First Alert and Honeywell Home branded air and safety products as evidenced by point-of-sale data across many of our key accounts. Demand for our newer products was enthusiastic, including our new highly rated combo smoke and carbon monoxide detector, purpose-built for easy installation while touting differentiated features and meeting the latest safety certification standards. Retail pricing strength reflected more efficient promotional spending, price increases and demand driven toward higher-margin products. Performance in the OEM combustion channel was also strong, reporting 9% revenue growth year-over-year against very strong results last year. Growth continues to be driven primarily by steady demand for higher-priced products.

From a geographic view, EMEA performance was a notable callout for the OEM combustion channel due to a seasonal build in advance of the upcoming heating season. Our distribution channel revenue was up 3% year-over-year, comprised of our 3 primary professional distribution channels, electrical, HVAC and security. Let me start with the electrical channel. The electrical distribution channel achieved record volume growth, resulting in double-digit percentage revenue growth year-over-year. We believe our position in the electrical channel has improved with several competitive conversions. Demand for new and existing BRK and Honeywell Home branded air and safety products was robust despite the current soft housing market.

We saw demand across all our electrical subsegments, including single-family and multifamily homes, manufactured housing and MRO. Our content per new residential built home continues to be nearly $400. The HVAC distribution channel grew revenue by a mid-single-digit percentage year-over-year, driven by both volume and price. The HVAC channel also achieved sequential revenue growth. Product demand was healthy from both our Americas and EMEA HVAC customers, especially for our newer, higher-value products such as dehumidifiers and connected thermostats. Our HVAC channel inventory balance remained stable over the last several months, consistent with the broader residential HVAC environment. Complementing the product demand in our HVAC channel was a solid uptick in our Pro-IQ service subscriptions.

These services, which are not yet material to our financial results, include software tools that professionals are using to improve the speed and quality of their installations, build homeowner loyalty and generate new business. Today's announcement of the addition of our AI-powered intelligence layer within Pro-IQ services is designed to proactively predict HVAC problems, demonstrating the continued value we are providing to professionals through our differentiated hardware and software intelligence. Revenue from the general security distribution channel was flat year-over-year, in line with the continued soft market for security installations, which are typically highly correlated with the resale of existing homes.

First, when we act as an outside design manufacturer for OEM security customers, the products we design and make for them are used to compete against ourselves in the general market. Second, OEM security sales generate less margin than our branded products. We believe selling a branded product in the general security marketplace where we can provide innovation and drive value is healthier for Resideo over the long term. I would like to reinforce how we are executing our strategy as a stand-alone company and highlight a few tangible examples of the progress we are making.

Our strategy is built around a powerful self-reinforcing cycle, investing in innovation to drive revenue growth, expanding margins through differentiated product design, continuously improving operational efficiency and reinvesting the benefits back into our innovation engine. And importantly, we are already seeing this strategy come to life. On innovation, our Elite Pro thermostats are a great example of how differentiated new products can drive growth with annualized revenue growth of approximately 50% since their introduction to the market. On margin expansion, our new combo smoke and carbon monoxide detector, which I spoke of earlier, is built on a redesigned common platform that improves product margins while delivering innovative features to our customers.

And on operational excellence, we are taking deliberate actions to simplify our business and improve efficiency, including SKU rationalization and the planned exit of 3 underutilized manufacturing facilities, including the announcement in the third quarter of the closure of our manufacturing operations in Scotland. These actions are designed to reduce our cost structure and improve utilization across our manufacturing footprint. Each of these initiatives reinforces the others. Innovation drives demand and creates opportunities for higher margins. Operational improvements further expand profitability and generate resources to reinvest in our next generation of products. This is the flywheel we are building at Resideo, innovation driving growth, growth and operational excellence, expanding profitability and those profits fueling the next wave of innovation.

We believe this self-reinforcing cycle will be a powerful driver of sustainable growth, margin expansion and long-term shareholder value. With that, let me turn the call over to Shane.

Shane Harrison: Thanks, Tom. I'd like to start by saying how thrilled I am to have joined the Resideo team. Over my first 2 months, I've had the opportunity to visit many of our sites, meet with our teams around the world and really dig into our products, operations and strategies. And what I've seen has only reinforced my excitement about the opportunity ahead. Resideo has iconic brands, accelerating product innovation and leading positions in many of the categories and geographies where we sell. The strong pipeline of product innovation is just beginning to deliver, and the company is filled with incredibly talented and passionate people who are energized by the opportunity to operate as a stand-alone product-focused company.

It's a powerful combination and one that I believe positions Resideo well for long-term growth, gross and EBITDA margin expansion and continued value creation. I'm excited to be part of this next chapter and to help the team realize the full potential of this business. Now on to the Q3 financial details. Third quarter gross margins were 40.4%, slightly higher than the third quarter of 2025. Drivers of gross margin expansion were price increases, operational efficiencies and $6 million of tariff refunds, which were partially offset by unfavorable product sales mix and inflationary input costs.

On inflationary input costs, we experienced an approximate $13 million year-over-year headwind to product input costs in the third quarter, which were partially offset by $3 million of benefits from the price increases we implemented this past June. Given notice periods for many of our customers, most price increases were not realized until the latter half of the third quarter. Stand-alone adjusted EBITDA was $154 million, representing growth of approximately 5% year-over-year, driven primarily by higher gross profit dollars and controlled operating expense growth. R&D continues to represent approximately 5% of total revenue as we invest behind new product launches and speed to market.

Stand-alone adjusted net income was $80 million and stand-alone adjusted earnings per share was $0.52, which excludes $30 million of nonrecurring business separation expenses recognized during the third quarter of 2026. Moving on to cash from operations. Total reported cash provided by continuing operations in the third quarter was $33 million versus the approximate $1.6 billion used for the termination of the indemnification agreement with Honeywell that occurred in the same period last year. Operating cash flow in the third quarter was negatively impacted by approximately $30 million of spin-related payments made during the quarter. Turning to the balance sheet. Our near-term priority after completion of the spin is deleveraging.

After receiving a onetime $900 million dividend from the spin-off of ADI, we repaid $1.1 billion of gross debt in the third quarter. We also made a $20 million payment at the end of the third quarter to ADI as part of the post-separation adjustment mechanism to true up ADI's cash. We anticipate further deleveraging and reinvestment in the business as Resideo continues to turn the flywheel and increase EBITDA and cash from operations. Before I provide our financial outlook for the fourth quarter and the full year 2026, I'd like to make some framing comments. First, we are flowing through our third quarter outperformance to our 2026 outlook while revising our outlook upward.

Second, after excluding OEM security, we currently expect fourth quarter revenue to be between flat and low single-digit growth year-over-year due to 4 less sales days in the fourth quarter, expected foreign currency exchange pressure and SKU rationalization. Third, included in our fourth quarter outlook is an approximate $30 million year-over-year reduction in OEM security revenue, resulting in revenue of approximately $25 million in the quarter, consistent with our previously communicated expectations. And fourth, on pricing and input cost inflation, we expect to realize the full benefit of the price increases implemented this past June during this fourth quarter.

However, continued inflationary pressures are expected to offset these benefits and result in a low single-digit million dollar cost headwind, which is reflected in our fourth quarter outlook and is consistent with our commentary in September. While we anticipate year-over-year gross margin growth in the fourth quarter, which we expect to be driven by the cost structure actions that Tom mentioned as well as continued volume growth from our core sales channels, we are also expecting a modest gross profit dollar reduction as a result of this inflationary environment and the expected lack of tariff refunds.

With that, for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect net revenue to be in the range of $710 million to $730 million, stand-alone adjusted EBITDA to be in the range of $145 million to $155 million, which is up slightly year-over-year at the midpoint, stand-alone adjusted earnings per share to be in the range of $0.42 to $0.48 and cash from operations to be at least $54 million.

For full year 2026, we expect net revenue to be in the range of $2.927 billion to $2.947 billion, stand-alone adjusted EBITDA to be in the range of $614 million to $624 million, which represents 21% of revenue, stand-alone adjusted earnings per share to be in the range of $1.92 to $1.98 and cash from operations to be at least $165 million for the full year. In closing, we remain focused on executing our strategy with discipline and consistency. While the macroeconomic environment remains dynamic, we believe our focus on these factors within our control positions Resideo to navigate these challenges.

The strong performance in our core channels in the third quarter, combined with our expected introduction of exciting new products in the fourth quarter underscores our confidence in the momentum that we are building as we enter 2027. As a stand-alone company, Resideo is now more focused on product innovation, growth acceleration and growing profitability, making it an exciting time for us and for our investors. We remain firmly committed to delivering on the long-term financial targets we outlined at our Investor Day. Let's now open the call up for questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is from the line of Erik Woodring of Morgan Stanley.

Erik Woodring: So Tom, I just want to start with you. Obviously, revenue, excluding that OEM security business grew 6% year-over-year despite kind of mixed housing market data point. Could you maybe just give us a little bit more color on growth by volume versus pricing? Just if you could contextualize for those for us, that would be super helpful. And then a quick follow-up, please.

Thomas Surran: Sure. Thanks for joining us tonight, Erik. It's a great question. So you're saying the core business, 6% year-over-year growth. You want a little more color commentary on what's going on with some of the business, it was a really solid quarter throughout the business. If you go through each of the segments, the distribution, the product areas, everything that is in our core business performed very well. And so you say, what about volume versus price?

If we extract out the OEM security and just look at our core business, our volume and price both increased, slightly more price because we had some of the inflationary costs, but we had very nice volume improvement, which is indicative of how we are performing in what you've described as a fairly tough market related to the housing. Now one of the reasons for that is what we provide, in many cases, is a nondiscretionary product, right? So this is the heating and cooling systems. This is the safety systems. This is the security system. These products are, again, nondiscretionary. And what we're seeing in the marketplace is us, what we perceive is gaining share in those markets.

Erik Woodring: That's awesome. Maybe just a follow-up to that is, obviously, there was news last month that Apple plans to get further into -- or I guess, let's say, get into the smart home market maybe rather than fighting against it. I guess from my perspective from the cheap seats, it looks like what they're trying to do is a little bit more DIY versus your obviously focused on the professional. But just any thoughts on what this could mean for Resideo and some of the products that you sell that might or might not be competition in that market? Thomas Surran: I would define it as creating an opportunity for us more than a competitive situation. But you're right, they play in a different place in the home. So they're about the engagement and the interaction and some of the automations on audio/video. That is not where we play. Where we focus is on the infrastructure systems of the house and making sure that the house is comfort and protectable.

So what we want to make sure, though, is that we're compatible with those systems, the smart home ecosystems of Apple, Amazon, Google. And so that's why we announced what we did. The fact is that if Apple is successful with this, they brought some new features, be it having customers understand and engage more with their critical systems, that will be great for us.

Alexander Virgo: I wondered if you could just unpick some of the differences in growth. The retail plus 15%, distribution plus 3% stands out to me as quite significantly different. Thomas Surran: Okay. So believe me or not, Alex, can you hear me okay? Yes. So they're pretty tied, your 2 questions that you just asked. It's a good question. If you carve that out, electrical distribution up 15%, HVAC distribution up 5% so we had and then OEM combustion up 10%. Alexander Virgo: That's very helpful. I wondered as a follow-up, if you could just give us a sense of how much the tariff refund helped the margin gross and EBITDA. But Apple has been a big advocate of Matter. And Matter is fantastic. Most of our -- in fact, all of our new smart home products support Matter. And that's great because we want that compatibility with those smart home ecosystems, and they all pretty much do support Matter. Where Matter is different, though, for us is it's great for that interchange. It's just not very deep for really controlling infrastructures.

Just the amount of information related to how a HVAC system works or how your safety systems need to have life safety protocols. That's just not something that's in a Matter protocol. So it's fantastic for interacting with the ecosystems and communicating information to the end user, but it's not something that we use deeply through our own system.

Aaron Kimson: Got it. That's really helpful. And then I know you mentioned Pro-IQ monetization is not material today, but can you help us think about the trajectory of monetization for the Pro-IQ Predict service? Will monetization be a recurring stream paid for by the buyer of the hardware? And is there a way to monetize it on the channel side by suggesting Pro to reach out to when something is looking like it's going to break?

Thomas Surran: Yes, that's exactly. So Aaron, let me just give a little background on Pro-IQ services. So we did announce Pro-IQ Predict today. But Pro-IQ services is actually a suite of services. And now we have 4 capabilities in that. The first one is install, and that basically gives the Pro the ability to do template and configuration in the field to be able to have a more efficient installation experience. The second one is engage. And this is about branding and contacts and booking for the Pro, so they can have their brand not only on the product space, but also in the app that the customer uses. Third is the analyze.

And this gives the Pro the ability to have alerts and look at trends and history of the product. And then what we announced now is Predict and this gives them the ability to diagnose potential problems, take preventative maintenance, but also if should something happen, they can understand what fails so they can make sure they bring the correct product part to make the repair to the customer, to make it a better experience for everyone, more efficient for them and certainly for the customer, a much simpler process. But all of this, it's really about creating stickiness with our customer and giving our customers value.

So that value and stickiness is our primary thought process as we think about Pro-IQ services. Right now, it's not material monetization, but it's delivering really nicely on that idea of the stickiness and how Pro's feel about the products we're bringing and the fact that we're bringing just a bit extra that they don't receive from other products.

Operator: The next question is from the line of Ian Zaffino of Oppenheimer.

Ian Zaffino: I just wanted to follow up on the tariff refunds. Did those kind of a surprise? And is there any other tariff refunds factored in forward guidance? I mean, or were you expecting, I guess, this kind of net $4 million in the third quarter?

Shane Harrison: So it's Shane. Nice to meet you. To answer your question, the short answer is we file for these refunds pretty far ahead of time. The visibility of when you get the money and if you're going to get the money, sometimes can be a little all over the place. So in this quarter, we did end up getting that $6 million and we ended up paying the couple out the door. So it was a net $4 million. So that's the answer there. But going forward for Q4, we have filed for more tariff refunds, but the visibility of seeing and getting those in is very, very murky.

So we -- in the guide that we just gave, we're assuming no tariff refunds or very little tariff refunds and probably a little bit coming out the door, but not anywhere like it used to be in the past.

Ian Zaffino: Okay. And then when we think about NPI is there a way you can maybe help us understand how well they're doing right now in the market? I know you had some introduced a while ago, maybe how those are performing? Thomas Surran: Okay, Ian. So how do we feel about NPI and how can you be aware of how they're performing? Having that platform out there is really important. And that's -- a lot of things were kind of bottled up a little bit behind it because we had to have the new platform in the market. And now we can start issuing out more and more products on top of that. There are products -- the reality is I'm telling you about how certain ones did.

But of the products we've released and the new products, we've been extremely pleased with how they've performed in the market. And sometimes we introduce products clearly for increasing revenue, but we also introduce products we've got to think about how they improve our margins. So that's a big driver of what they do. There's also reasons to sometimes shore up a strategic position on making sure that we don't have a competitive weakness and also making sure that our products have the depth that really is unmatched by our competition.

Because when you look at our products, it's not only the headline product, it's everything it attaches to so that Pro can get the job done when they're at the house and doing it. So we want to make sure some of these smaller products we introduce, you say, well, why did they do that? It's not going to move. It's that solution for the professional. And that's what he has -- why he has trusted us is because we give that. So we're clearly going to introduce NPI to drive revenue growth. We're going to introduce products that improve our cost profile.

We're going to introduce products that have strategic importance and basically make sure that Pro has a complete solution.

Operator: The next question is from the line of Tomo Sano of JPMorgan.

Tomohiko Sano: So you noted that unfavorable mix and input cost inflation partially offset margin gains. How do you expect those headwinds to change in the fourth quarter and beyond, please?

Shane Harrison: Tomo, it's Shane. I'll take that one. So in Q3, you heard us say it was about a $13 million headwind on the inflation cost in the quarter. And then we offset that with about $3 million of realized price increases. Well, that's -- so net $10 million, let's call it, as a headwind. As we move into Q4 in the guidance we just gave, there is an assumption there that the inflation costs are still going to continue, probably even a little bit higher, but we had a lot more price realization, the price increase realization from our June increases. So the net increase is going to be lower than what we saw in Q3.

So less of a headwind, let's call it, for Q4.

Tomohiko Sano: And a follow-up to Tom. And have you seen any changes in competitors' pricing or promotional activities? How is Resideo's differentiation helping you sustain pricing and protect market share?

Thomas Surran: Sure. So right now, obviously, it's a season where there's some customers or some competitors are doing promotional pricing. But our pricing, we typically don't do a heavy promotional pricing because our pricing is typically related and driven by the needs of the professional. And they're basically executing in accordance with the needs for jobs. They have assignments, they're going to the house, they're doing work and promotional just seems to be not something that's appropriate at that place. In terms of our pricing, we believe we still deliver the best value out there in the marketplace.

When you look at our products and the value that they provide and the pricing that we're asking, we think we stand at the top of the chart on basically bang for the buck.

Operator: The next question is from the line of Jay Goldberg of Seaport.

Jay Goldberg: Tom, I guess first question for you. You've talked a lot about new products coming out next year. And I'm wondering -- I know you're going to talk about this more at your event next week. It's super interesting. But I was wondering, to what degree have you sort of shown this to some group of Pro customers? And what's the response you're getting from the new directions, the new products you're getting from the Pros? And I have a follow-up.

Thomas Surran: So Jay, you're right. And again, thank you for joining us. And so I will say that, yes, we do get a little bit of a sneak preview of how the customers are going to respond because we have beta programs in many cases. And some of the products that will be discussed at the upcoming Connect 2026 Conference have been through beta. And we know what the feedback from the several hundred of the Pros that have tried some of these products, and it's been very positive. So we have a pretty good idea of how they'll be received, at least some of the things that have actually gone through beta.

I think in general, if you're going to be at Connect 2026, it will be great to be able to get the feedback from the Pros about how they feel the NPI that we've brought to market and how it's executing for them.

Jay Goldberg: Okay. And then my follow-up will be for Shane. I guess I was just hoping like this quarter, your revenue came in above where -- or pretty close to where I was expecting it, but you were much more profitable. And I'm just wondering, as we're thinking -- building out our models for next year, how should we think about operating leverage? It seems to be moving in your favor. Is that safe to say?

Shane Harrison: Yes, that's the right way to think about it. As we laid out a model at Investor Day back in whatever that was, July, I believe. The model there is -- I'm going to remind you of the model because it's something I love to talk about. So at the top line, we're expecting mid-single-digit growth annually over this 5-year period through 2030 now that's not going to be linear. But this year, according to our guide, we're going to be right at that, right, [ 4.4 ] if you take out that OEM -- the OEM security headwind. You move down the stack from there, you look at gross margin.

We're also expecting around point of gross margin improvement every year throughout the 2030. But for every point that we do gain on gross margin, we're going to throw another probably 50 points of that into R&D, kind of back to the flywheel concept that we talked about and Tom talked about in the prepared remarks. But then to build that operating leverage below that, it's controlled overhead and SG&A spending that will drive another point, call it, similar to what we're seeing in gross margin but at the EBITDA level.

And if you do that math over that 5-year period, you're going to see what I love, which is a mid-single digit up into the mid- to high single digit and then high single-digit EBITDA growth. And that's what we want to see, and that's what we're going to plan. Now for 2027, we're right in the middle of budget season. So I don't think that what the numbers look like right now, but I can tell you that's what we're striving for. And it's that flywheel that Tom brought up is real, and we do believe that, that is going to be a very giant enabler of getting this operating leverage that I just talked about.

Jay Goldberg: Very helpful. And then just one last little nit. If I understand it right, your revenue guidance for next year is basically in line with what you laid out at the Analyst Day a month ago, but you're hitting that even though you no longer have the security OEM business. So on a like-for-like basis, you're effectively raising guidance a little bit?

Shane Harrison: So you're talking about for '26, the '26 guide?

Shane Harrison: Yes, yes. So yes, what we did is we outperformed in Q3. We're going to pass that through. We're going to flow that right through, and we're going to -- we're keeping the implied Q4 guide and actually raising it slightly at the midpoint. So yes, you're seeing a full year '26 guide increase. And frankly, what we're seeing with our forecasting in Q4 is very similar to what we were seeing 3 months ago, which is why we're kind of keeping that implied guide for Q4 where it's at. And then yes, flowing through that Q3.

#3002. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.
