#2999. Grocery Outlet (GO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Sales growth returned as opportunistic deals rebuilt store traffic.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Grocery Outlet Holding Corp. (GO +1.08%) reported a return to positive comparable store sales in the third quarter, driven by a strategic pivot back to its core opportunistic procurement model. Management stated that the company successfully transitioned away from the broad-based synthetic promotions utilized earlier in the year as the volume of high-value branded deals in the supply chain recovered. The company reported a sequential acceleration in traffic and maintained its expansion pace with 14 new store openings. While gross margins faced pressure from elevated freight and a regional produce health event, management indicated that underlying trends in October suggest momentum is building heading into the fourth quarter. The company revised its full-year guidance to reflect these improved sales trends while tightening EBITDA expectations to account for lumpy maintenance costs and supply chain headwinds.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Grocery Outlet's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Nicolo Cottarelli, Senior Vice President of Strategic Finance and Investor Relations. Thank you. You may begin.

Nicolo Cottarelli: Good afternoon, and welcome to Grocery Outlet's call to discuss financial results for the third quarter ended October 3, 2026. Speaking for management on today's call will be Jason Potter, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Ian Ferry, Chief Financial Officer. Following prepared remarks from Jason and Ian, we will open the call for questions. Please note that this conference call is being webcast live, and a recording will be available via playback on the Investor Relations section of the company's website. Participants on this call may make forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. All statements that address future operating, financial, or business performance, or the company's strategies or expectations are forward-looking statements.

These forward-looking statements are subject to various risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements. Description of these factors can be found in this afternoon's press release, as well as in the company's periodic reports filed with the SEC, all of which may be found on the Investor Relations section of the company's website or on sec.gov. The company undertakes no obligation to revise or update any forward-looking statements or information. These statements are estimates only and not a guarantee of future performance. Additionally, during today's call, the company will reference certain non-GAAP financial information, including adjusted items.

Reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP measures, as well as the description, limitations, and rationale for using each measure, may be found in the supplemental financial tables included in this afternoon's press release on the Investors section of the company's website under News and Releases and in the company's SEC filings. Now I would like to turn it over to Jason.

Jason Potter: Good afternoon to you all, and thank you for joining us for our quarterly update. Our results improved in the third quarter, with a return to positive comps driven by our focus on executing an enhanced opportunistic assortment. Revenue increased 0.9% to $1.18 billion, with comparable store sales up 50 basis points. That was an 80 basis point improvement from the comp sales we reported for Q2, despite the adverse headwind from the Cyclospora outbreak during the third quarter. Comp was driven by a 2.4% increase in traffic, representing a 60 basis point sequential improvement from Q2. It was partially offset by a 1.9% decrease in basket, which was a 20 basis point sequential improvement from Q2.

Gross margin of 30% was within our outlook range, reflecting slightly less promotional spend than was expected, but slightly greater than anticipated pressure on freight. Adjusted EBITDA of $59.4 million landed in the middle of our guidance range, and adjusted EPS at $0.16 at the high end, which Ian will discuss further. These results demonstrate continued progress in our efforts to revitalize Grocery Outlet's value proposition and drive sustainable growth. We're committed to reinforcing our position as a leading value retailer, and we are excited about what that progress means for our customers and communities, especially in this challenging economic environment.

I'll begin today with more detail about our comp sales improvement and the critical link that improving our opportunistic product assortment execution had during Q3. I'll also share updates on how we're improving collaboration with our suppliers and supporting our operators in this focused effort. And I'll finish by sharing how we see the business developing through the end of the year. First, delivering comp improvement. Our progress on comp continues to be supported by continuing traffic growth, demonstrating that our focus on executing an improved opportunistic assortment and continued emphasis on value communication is drawing more customers into our stores.

As inflation continues to pressure household budgets and more shoppers cite value as their top purchase criteria, we're working to ensure our offering is increasingly relevant. During the quarter, our prices on everyday assortment remained competitive, and our retail inflation has tracked below the broader market. During the quarter, we continued to shift our mix to higher levels of opportunistic product, creating greater absolute value and savings across the basket as a result. We see encouraging evidence that this focus is resonating with customers.

Customer credit card data indicates that Q3 traffic growth was driven by an increase in the number of new customers, and we're also gaining traction in e-commerce, where our implementation of parity pricing has resulted in driving incremental sales and positive margin dollars. While economic conditions continue to pressure our customer basket down year-on-year, positive sequential trends in basket size and the underlying units per transaction show we are making progress as we strengthen our assortment and overall execution. Notably, year-on-year opportunistic units per transaction growth was positive in Q3, as customers are responding to the more compelling assortment in our stores. These efforts are strengthening our brand and contributing to positive improvements in customer NPS scores year-on-year.

In August, we also celebrated Grocery Outlet's 80th anniversary with targeted marketing that emphasized our improving slate of opportunistic deals. The 3-day event saw double-digit comps across the company and generated strong units per transaction growth. It's a useful example of how we have transitioned this year from broad-based synthetic promotions to now surgically deploying investments to drive more engagement from our customers. Our operators executed at a high level, and it was great to celebrate 80 years of both serving our customers and communities. Our comp progress was achieved despite the impact of the Cyclospora outbreak.

While none of our products were involved in any of the Cyclospora recalls, the resulting impact on our produce business reduced total company comp by roughly 60 basis points during the third quarter. This was less than the 100 basis point impact we anticipated based on the data we had in front of us at the time of our Q2 call. Increased produce shrink also compressed overall gross margins slightly. With that noted, we've seen a nice recovery in both comps and margin in produce, and the category has been growing at above inflation since the start of October.

Our buying team and stores are ready to capitalize on the returning demand, and we expect no lingering impact of Cyclospora through the rest of the year. With this effect subsiding, overall company comps were positive in September and have accelerated into October. Returning to positive comp is an important marker of our progress, but the goal is to improve comps further and sustain those gains. To sustain our comp performance improvement, we remain laser-focused on continuing to prioritize execution improvements in our opportunistic assortment, and then sharing these amazing branded deals with our customers to consistently deliver excitement and discovery in every store.

I'll now turn to how we execute against that priority in Q3 and the work to come as we close out this year. On revitalizing our opportunistic assortment. As we discussed, our primary goal since the start of this year has been to strengthen our opportunistic assortment, given its foundational and differentiating role in the Grocery Outlet customer value proposition. We've activated the entire organization in this effort, starting with our buying and merchandising teams, and partnering with our suppliers and collaborating with our independent operators. We've made some important trade-offs. One example is to reduce elements of our everyday assortment to ensure we make the space for opportunistic products in our supply chain and at the shelf.

By sourcing more exciting opportunistic deals and merchandising them with excellence, we drove a meaningful improvement in opportunistic comp and mix during the third quarter. All of that in turn value for our customers. We are seeing this cycle of improvement show up in terms of positive value satisfaction, customer growth, and strengthening baskets. As we shared last quarter, we began this transformation with a specific set of actions to improve the opportunistic assortment for the grocery department. This process and focus drove grocery back to healthy levels of growth in Q2, which was sustained through the third quarter.

During the early part of Q3, the team turned to repeating that same focused approach to both the frozen and deli departments. We're pleased to share that the same repeatable process is proving highly effective. Opportunistic mix increased materially in both departments over the quarter, and the department comp has followed. As we move forward, we intend to maintain our methodical, focused approach to growing and maintaining the opportunistic assortment, working our way through the departments in a manner that allows us to deliver the right level of value, excitement, and novelty with our customers. This is supported by improved signage and updated digital outreach, including our new, more shoppable website and more focused messaging on deals and discovery.

We're confident that customers will continue to respond to this renewed and more exciting experience. During Q3, our approach to collaboration and support with our suppliers and operators has also proved effective. As customers respond to the work we're doing in our stores, we're also actively engaging with our independent operators and suppliers. In Q3, we hosted a series of regional roadshows and workshops across the country, giving us the opportunity to connect in person with our operators. We continue to hear positive feedback about the new tools, processes, and improvements we've introduced earlier this year, and I continue to be impressed with the collaboration, dedication, and commitment to drive growth and profitability that our operators demonstrate every day.

We've seen our IOs average income increase year-to-date versus last year as a result of this work, an important indicator for the improving health of the business and operator engagement. In early Q4, we hosted our second Supplier Summit of the Year, creating the perfect opportunity to work with our supplier partners to expand our business opportunities together. These valuable summits generate deal flow, generate new business, help improve execution, and build and reinforce strong relationships. This increased engagement with operators and suppliers creates meaningful opportunities for collaboration and getting the business back to the levels of growth we know we can all achieve together.

We look forward to continuing to partner with our operators and our suppliers to drive performance improvement across the business. As discussed earlier this year, we remain committed to operational discipline and effective capital deployment. Our store refresh and new store programs continue at the measured pace we previously outlined. Finally, our strategic review of the UGO business remains ongoing, and we don't have anything new to share at this time. Now, looking to Q4. Before closing, I'd like to take a moment to share some high-level expectations for the fourth quarter. We believe the positive trends we're seeing coming out of Q3 and into Q4 bode well for sales growth and our comp trajectory.

We've wound down the synthetic promotional spending we introduced earlier this year, as our opportunistic assortments, current weight, depth, and quality is now providing significant value and excitement for our customers. We've learned much during this last year, and we'll stay flexible in deploying targeted promotions where we have a high confidence in driving traffic, or for those promotions that create broader benefits, like our recent successful 80th anniversary celebration that I mentioned. For Q4, we're making a similar surgical investment into our Thanksgiving promotion that we believe will contribute to overall sales performance for this quarter and benefit subsequent periods by increasing the engagement of our most loyal customers.

While that planned promotion and some cost pressures in our supply chain that are embedded in the gross margin guidance that Ian will share, we feel confident in our ability to manage margin responsibly and in our ability to expand margins over time. That said, we're remaining diligent and focused on operational discipline as we aim to drive durable, profitable growth. In closing, we're encouraged by the results of the quarter, but have much left to do before we're satisfied with our performance. Our #1 priority continues to be strengthening our opportunistic assortment, which we believe will unlock higher levels of comp growth. We'll continue to optimize and refine our operations to promote growth and drive efficiency across our business.

In an environment where value is essential to our customers, our model is uniquely positioned to serve, and we see continued evidence of that in our financial performance. I'm confident in our ability to achieve our goals, and with a stronger foundation, we're well-positioned to capture on our long-term opportunities. We look forward to updating you on how we finish out this year. I'd like to thank our customers, our operators, our team, and our shareholders. Our focus lies firmly in delivering value to all of you. And with that, I'll turn it over to Ian. Ian?

Ian Ferry: Thanks, Jason. In the third quarter, we saw a return to positive comps and delivered financial results in line with our guidance as we continue to strengthen the foundation of the business. Our efforts to restore and enhance the attributes that make this business unique and differentiated are starting to resonate with consumers and drive sales improvement. As we build on the sales trends, we'll continue to spend with discipline and expect to improve our profitability and return on capital over time. I will start with the quarter and then discuss our fourth quarter and full year outlook. Unless otherwise noted, the comparisons I provide are year-over-year. Starting with the top line.

Third quarter net sales increased 0.9% to $1.18 billion. Positive comparable store sales and sales from stores opened over the last 12 months more than offset the impact of the Optimization Plan store closures earlier this year. We opened 14 stores and closed 0 during the quarter. Comparable store sales increased 50 basis points, ahead of our guidance of negative 1% to flat. The improvement reflected 2 factors: a smaller-than-anticipated headwind from Cyclospora and stronger traffic and basket driven by our strategy to enhance the opportunistic assortment. On Cyclospora, we guided to 100 basis point impact on Q3 comp, but we came in approximately 40 basis points favorable to that estimate.

We continue to see evidence that our focus on the opportunistic assortment is driving traffic and sales. We are encouraged by customer credit card data showing sequential growth in the active number of customers shopping our stores, demonstrating traction in attracting shoppers. Notwithstanding the pressure on the basket, which is impacted by broader economic conditions, sequential improvement on basket and positive results on opportunistic units per transaction growth show that we are making progress. Gross profit trended slightly favorable to expectations in Q3, with gross margin of 30.0% coming in at the high end of our outlook. Gross profit dollars of $353 million were down slightly year-over-year, and gross margin was down 40 basis points year-over-year.

The decline was contemplated in our outlook and reflected pressures we experienced during the quarter, including the impact of the supplemental promotional spend introduced this year, higher supply chain costs, and increased produce shrink related to the Cyclospora outbreak, and was partially offset by the favorable shift in opportunistic mix. We spent less than we expected on our synthetic promotional investments in Q3, notwithstanding investments in the 80th anniversary celebration. GAAP SG&A increased slightly to $332.5 million, and as a percentage of net sales, declined 10 basis points to 28.2%.

Sequentially, GAAP SG&A improved 30 basis points as a percentage of net sales, primarily driven by lower incentive compensation and professional fees, partially offset by higher costs to support our business growth. We also recorded $3.6 million in net restructuring credits related to the Optimization Plan. This included $15.8 million in noncash credits, primarily from the net write-off of lease right-of-use assets and lease liabilities, partially offset by $12.2 million in cash charges. Below the operating line, net interest expense was $7 million, up 5.1% from last year. Our GAAP effective tax rate was 21.8% compared with 28% last year.

Net income was $13.3 million, or $0.13 per diluted share, compared with $11.6 million, or $0.12 per diluted share last year. Adjusted net income was $15.6 million, or $0.16 per diluted adjusted share, compared with $20.7 million, or $0.21 per diluted adjusted share last year. Adjusted EBITDA was $59.4 million, or 5% of net sales, compared with $66.7 million, or 5.7% of net sales last year. Adjusted EBITDA came in at the middle of our outlook range, while adjusted EPS came in at the high end. Turning to the balance sheet and cash flow statement. We ended the quarter with $59.8 million in cash and approximately $154 million of revolver availability.

Total debt net of issuance costs was $502 million, down $3.7 million from Q2. Net leverage was 1.9x adjusted EBITDA at quarter end. Operating cash flow was $18.2 million compared with $17.3 million last year. The increase was driven primarily by higher accrued and other liabilities due primarily to timing, partially offset by lower operating lease liabilities as a result of the Optimization Plan. Capital expenditures were $28.1 million, or $25.7 million net of tenant improvement allowances. Now, onto our outlook. Our fourth quarter guidance contemplates continued improvement in comp as we drive further execution on our opportunistic initiatives.

Our margin outlook reflects the step down of our promotional work from prior quarters, balanced with some headwinds that we are managing. We are also expecting some pressure in SG&A, driven by higher repairs and maintenance expenses on our fleet and other line items. As a reminder, last year's fourth quarter included a 53rd week in the 2025 fiscal year, adding $82.4 million to net sales and $9 million to adjusted EBITDA. Our fourth quarter and full year outlook reflect the absence of those benefits this year.

For the fourth quarter, we expect comparable store sales ranging from positive 1.5% to 2.5%, gross margin of 29.7% to 30.0%, adjusted EBITDA of $57 million to $61 million, and diluted adjusted EPS of $0.11 to $0.14 per share. For the full year, we now expect net new store openings of 30 to 31 stores, net sales of $4.7 billion to $4.72 billion, comparable store sales in the range of positive 0.2% to 0.4%, gross margin of 29.8% to 30%, adjusted EBITDA of $225 million to $229 million, diluted adjusted EPS of $0.52 to $0.55, and capital expenditures net of tenant improvement allowances of $170 million.

In summary, we're confident in our ability to build off the results of the work we've done this year and drive towards sustainable, profitable growth. Near-term, we remain focused on getting more opportunistic product into our stores across more departments, ensuring our value proposition is well communicated to customers, and managing the business with discipline. Echoing Jason, thanks to everyone across the business and to our shareholders. We look forward to updating you at the end of our fiscal year. With that, I'll turn the call over to the operator for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question today, we'll hear from Robby Ohmes with Bank of America.

Robert Ohmes: My first question just would be for Jason, just the -- sorry if you did this already, but the delivery pricing change with parity pricing, did that hit this quarter, and did you see any significant changes in delivery and things like that? Maybe Instacart, DoorDash merging, could that have an impact on your delivery business?

Jason Potter: Sure. Robby, thanks for the question. First thing I'll say is, we do believe the business will continue to generate positive in-store traffic and comp growth of over 3% over time, irrespective of what we're doing online. That said, we did, as we indicated before, implemented price parity. And in doing that, the reason, the rationale for it was to make sure that the customer, the consumer could see our pricing and understand the offering online. That's been successful. We're really happy with the results. Their ability to see that value is translated into larger baskets and an inflow of new customers. We can kind of see that in the reporting.

As we indicated, or what I will share is, it is margin dilutive, obviously, taking fees off and creating price parity, but the results are EBITDA positive. So, we're excited with those changes as they are at this point. It's a small part of our business. And your follow-up question on DoorDash, Instacart, it's early days. We're unsure of what that means, but both great partners, and we expect that great partnership to continue.

Robert Ohmes: And just a quick follow-up. How are you thinking about longer term, a time line to get the business back to sort of a 6% or higher EBITDA margin? What are sort of the 2 or 3 key things that need to happen?

Jason Potter: Yes, Robby, thanks for the question. We're still in the relative early innings. Our priority this year was to make sure that we were focusing on improving value by improving price perception through our opportunistic assortment. I would tell you that we're excited about the progress there with the team. On that part of the business, to get comps moving and obviously get back to a more normal level of profitability, we've seen op comp accelerate meaningfully through Q3. Our mix continues to expand. The playbook that Paul Miller and the team have put in place for grocery sustained itself through Q3. We've seen improvement across deli and frozen as we've turned our attention there.

And so, I think on the value component, what I would hope to be able to do in the next call is to give you an update on where we are there. We're likely kind of halfway through on that piece of the business. That work will continue meaningfully through next year. The value piece being the key priority of our offering is essential. And then when we look at the business, our customers have been clear about what else they need. It's also clear to us that the customer experience is important.

And so, as we work on things like improving our fresh offering, in-stocks, store standards, and so on, that we'll see the basket growth, I think, rebound and start to grow. And our expectation is, as we improve the business and continue to execute, loyalty will improve, and ultimately, we'll get the business back to where we know it can achieve.

Operator: Next, we'll move to Edward Kelly with Wells Fargo.

Edward Kelly: I wanted to ask you about the guidance and the implied Q4 guidance. So comp coming in a little bit better than expected, that guide comes up. Q3 EBITDA was in line with expectation, but I think the implied Q4 comes down a bit, I guess, with what you did with the full year EBITDA guide. Can you just maybe talk a little bit more about what's impacting that? And then how much of that sort of carries into 2027? And then, I guess, like how close are you to sort of run rate of what EBITDA should look like as you get into next year?

Ian Ferry: Ed, it's Ian. Thanks for the question. So just to start out at a high level, as Jason said, our focus this year has been on driving comp acceleration through revitalizing the op pipeline. So in the end of Q3, we exited the quarter at a comp rate that was 400 basis points higher than where we were in January. So that feels good, and clearly we're guiding to further improvement in Q4. Meanwhile, we do think we've aligned on a healthier approach to gross margin as we've moved through the year and tapered the promotional bridge that we put in place back in January.

So for Q3, you're right, we did outperform on both comp and gross margin rate, which contributed about $2 million of upside, and that was offset by $2 million of unfavorable SG&A pressure. That came predominantly from elevated repairs and maintenance, so about $1 million, and then the rest just from a handful of discrete items. And it's a similar story as you move into Q4. There's probably about $1 million of upside versus the prior implied guide from comp outperformance. And we're guiding to a $3 million lower midpoint.

So, when you look at the $4 million net pressure on SG&A, again, a very big chunk of that is just elevated repairs and maintenance, which are just coming in much lumpier than what the budget had, and a handful of discrete items. So, not really expecting that to repeat into next year, but net-net, we're happy with the performance and where we're looking at for Q4.

Edward Kelly: Okay. And just a follow-up. You mentioned that the promotional bridge is ending. You had some other promo around the 80th anniversary, and then you have Thanksgiving coming up. I'm just kind of curious, as the promotional stuff's rolling off and you think about like these more normal weeks, how would you gauge the underlying momentum of the business as the promotion has been rolling off? And then as part of that, could you just maybe dissect basket a bit? I'm just kind of curious, is basket turning sort of the way that you thought that it would? Is it a little bit slower? Just curious as to how you're thinking about that sequential change.

Ian Ferry: Yes. Ed, I'll take the first part and then shift the basket commentary to Jason. On the promotional spend, we did consistently taper it throughout the year as we got more effective on running promotions, as well as just restoring op mix. And in fact, in October, we had no excess promotion in the system, and comps accelerated month-over-month. So we felt good about that. And in aggregate, we spent certainly less than $20 million that we had planned, and think it would be unlikely that we would repeat that or move that back into the program as we look at next year.

Jason Potter: Yes, Ed, just to answer your question on basket, I'll hit a few points here. First and foremost, the basket has improved a couple hundred basis points from the start of the year. We're happy to see that recovery. There was some improvement as well, Q3 from Q2 overall, and that was really driven by units per transaction from our op focus. So what we're seeing in the baskets is a higher degree of op. That's, obviously, showing up in a number of places, improving the value in the basket. And so, as I mentioned, the question that Robby asked, happy to see the basket improving.

As we continue to execute and improve the business, I do expect to see basket growth in addition to traffic growth. So what we are seeing right now is a consistent ability to generate traffic, but a lagging basket. And I think the continued work we're doing, the focus, it's clear that's working. We're going to continue that work through next year. And as we improve the other side of value, which is the customer experience piece, we're going to see basket growth.

Operator: And Corey Tarlowe with Jefferies will have our next question.

Corey Tarlowe: Jason, you've mentioned a few times the benefit that the business has realized from the change in strategy this year around opportunistic product. I was wondering if you could provide a little bit more detail or quantification around the magnitude of that benefit when a certain number of products or percentage of products are in the store. Do you notice any sort of critical mass forming? I want to just have a better understanding, if possible, of how tangible these benefits are. And what the ultimate runway could look like for this?

Jason Potter: Sure, Corey. Great question. Thanks for asking. Op has been the value and sales-generating engine of the business for some time. It's our source of differentiation, obviously. And the areas that we see tangible evidence, it's across a host of KPIs, but we know that the degree of op we have in the business and its comp performance is correlated with comp sales. Mix matters, so the improvements we have made several hundred basis points year-to-date on mix demonstrates a weight, a range of products.

So, your point about how many items in store, we are measuring that, and we do measure what do we have every day, what do we have in op, that does matter across the network, and the quality as well. And so, we do have measures on quality, things like brand strength and so on, to help us understand what that looks like. We also measure things like the discount, the actual pricing, how that shows up in the basket, and then things like turns. There is a newness and discovery to this, that flow is important.

Making sure we continue to be relevant across the network is important, so we are also manage and monitor the SKUs that are unique in different markets. We don't always have an item that covers every single store, so that's also important. All of that to say, I think by the time we have the call, the next call will likely be halfway through the work. And I think this work will continue well into next year. But there is a clear relationship for us that we see with the performance of this part of the business and the overall performance of the core of the business.

And so, the improvements we've seen, especially I would say notable is October, our comp run rate has now exited at a very nice kind of high end of the range that we gave for Q4, all driven by op. So, that synthetic promotion was gone, and again, the value piece that's driven from price perception and value comes from that part of the business. So, excited about what we're doing, but there is more to do, Corey.

Corey Tarlowe: And then I was just wondering if you could provide a little bit color on pricing. With fuel prices being what they are, how are you thinking about pricing as we head into next year?

Jason Potter: Yes. No, that's a great question. And it's on everyone's minds, obviously. I would tell you that our pricing gaps are stable. We're monitoring that across the major MSAs. We look at that every day. We do see inflation on everyday assortment. That's something we're managing. We're passing through appropriately to manage the gaps that we have. That's been straightforward for the team. I think the benefits of what we've done with op and extending its mix and its reach, the AURs are lower. People that come in our stores are getting more value with more items in a basket of goods, especially in a period like this. And our ability to maintain the gaps is there.

The team has an agility to move sources of supply, which we've done this year in some cases. And again, the continued work on the mix has been especially helpful during this period. So, as far as we're concerned, we're managing inflation appropriately, and the team has the tools to get it done.

Operator: And next we'll hear from John Heinbockel with Guggenheim Partners.

John Heinbockel: So, Jason, do you think when you look at op comp versus every day, and I don't know if you look at it that way, where we are today, op comp should lead every day because you are driving traffic on an improved value proposition? Is that fair? And then I think historically, right, the op margins were quite a bit higher. Do you want to run the business that way? Or if the mix is higher, you can provide more value and earn a little bit less margin?

Jason Potter: Yes. Thanks for the question, John. It's a good question. So we do monitor different categories of product growth. Op comp has clearly been running faster than the MTO part of our business. That's by design. As the team has continued to improve inventory flow, new supplier acquisition, engagement with our existing suppliers, that's worked really nicely in the business and also really fights inflation effects, if you will, on a basket of goods. So the more op we drive, the higher mix of quality op that's available, and you always have to turn the product. People want newness in the store, and that's important.

Those things are very healthy for the business, and they drive traffic, and they drive comps. And so, we're going to continue to manage the business on the value side when it comes to price. If you kind of break value, there's price, there's quality, and customer experience. The price part of what our work is the priority right now, and that work is clearly paying some early dividends and getting the momentum back into the business. The second part of your question on margin, there is a clear margin advantage. It's accretive for us. Every op item we sell versus an MTO item is more profitable.

We do have to manage the business as well to make sure that we have enough everyday assortment to meet a broad-based set of needs that customers have. And so, as we move to next year and work on things like better inventory management tools, those kinds of things will also help us build the basket. But op will remain a central focus of the team and our #1 priority throughout next year.

John Heinbockel: And then my follow-up is, I know you guys had some work you were doing, right, on store layout and format, and I think that was kind of pulled back a little bit. When do you think the top line is sustainable enough where you go back and the IOs want to put some more capital? Or where you put more capital into the stores?

Jason Potter: Yes, no, that's a great question, John. Thank you. We are wanting to go at a certain pace here. I think we've moderated that with new stores. We've moderated that with some of the conversation we had around those refresh to make sure that everyone in the organization was focused on the price part of value, which our customers were telling us clearly we had needed to do some work on. So that will likely continue well into next year.

I think when we get enough momentum behind us and consistency in results, we'll make sure that at that point, we'll turn our attention to those kinds of opportunities, which are still there and provide a lot of headroom for the business. So we're still excited about what those things mean. Some of what we did this year with making the stores easier to shop has shown up in positive feedback from customers and is also helping the digital experience for people that are coming into our stores for the first time. So those things are there, they're present, they're available. Our operators have a good understanding now of what's to come.

But again, our focus is going to be to continue to work this part of the business, make sure that's dialed in, and the team there is working hard to create a repeatable set of processes to make sure that this continues. Again, we're excited about the progress, but more to come.

Operator: And next, we'll hear from Mark Carden with UBS.

Mark Carden: So as you look across your shopper base, to what extent did you see your comp vary across your lower, middle, and higher-income customer cohorts? Are you seeing much in the way of impacts from mass merchants who are doing their own discounting, even if it's not as deep as yours? And then, are you seeing the new customers you were referencing skewing any higher or lower income?

Jason Potter: Yes. Mark, thanks. It's Jason. Well, I appreciate the question. I think your question relates to potential trade down. Couple things I'll say. We think this business is built to succeed in any economic backdrop, and we've had cycles before where things have been pressured for the consumer, and this business pops. We think the work we're doing right now positions us well for that. Couple different stories just to tell, I think, on this point. So on the first point, on the customer pressure, I think for the first time in Q3, I saw some evidence.

We see it in the basket, but we're looking at things like substitution, and we could see in fresh protein a fair bit of pressure in premium beef. I think everyone's well aware of the inflation effects that have happened with the cattle shortage, and that started to show up in what we see in that particular category. That said, we have been looking for evidence of trade down, and this is very thin data at this point, but when we're looking at our credit card data, the new customers that are coming in, we are seeing a slight uptick in premium credit cards. But again, it's not significant enough for us to really make a judgment.

And I think it's kind of still up in the air. But again, our priority here is to return the model to a best-in-class value offering. And again, we're really laser-focused on the price part of that and executing everyday value and making sure that our op is healthy and growing.

Mark Carden: And then as a follow-up, you opened 14 new stores in 3Q. You guys have been making some adjustments to your opening strategy. How did new store productivity track on these stores relative to where you'd like to be? And then, how is the IO pipeline shaping up relative to what you've seen in the past?

Jason Potter: Yes. A couple of things to say there. Number one, we're still excited about the long-term unit growth opportunity for Grocery Outlet. As a reminder for those of you that maybe are new to this or just to hit it one more time, we have slowed down the pace of new store growth and shifted our mix of store execution on infill, and we did that to make sure that we're improving the rate and consistency of returns. So, again, just as a reminder, in the last 3 years, the company opened roughly a 50/50 mix, new market to infill.

And just to add to the answer to the question you're asking, the '25 cohort is on track with our performance. The '26 group is kind of 2/3 infill with a balanced new market. What I'm seeing right now is, for the '26 group, and again the year's not up, infill is largely on track, but I am seeing variability in new markets. And so, we will have some work to do when we do come back around in the midterm to new market growth, refining our process there. In the short-term for '27, our plan is to execute roughly 20 net new openings.

They're all infill, and again, that gives us confidence in the predictability and support of the returns that we're going to generate.

Operator: And next we'll hear from Leah Jordan with Goldman Sachs.

Leah Jordan: I just want to stick to the new store growth outlook first. We've been hearing about some tight supply across retail real estate and strip centers and the like, and it sounds like you've got visibility on the 20 new stores for next year. But maybe just -- what you're seeing in your markets that you're looking at around supply, visibility there for the pipeline for the next couple of years as you start to build that out. And then, maybe an update on unit economics. How are those potentially higher costs, right, if it's a tighter supply, flowing through and impacting your unit economics as you build out those new stores?

Jason Potter: Leah, thanks for the question. On the first part of your question, haven't seen direct evidence of that tightness. Some of what we've seen, there was something in the -- there was a lot of drug stores available, and we're seeing a fair bit of open retail. So not saying that's not the case, but just haven't had that experience here at this point. I think I'll pass part 2 of the question on to Ian just to sort of address.

Ian Ferry: Yes. Leah, on the unit economics, I mean, you're right. They have come down over the last several years as construction costs have become elevated and CapEx required has gone up. When the company went public, these were, call it, 4-wall, 4-year returns in excess of 35%, and it's more recently been something closer to 20% to 25%. There's also this dynamic where our new markets have kind of varied from plan, whereas, as Jason said, on an infill basis, even with all the challenges we've had as a business, have actually been very consistent in recent years in terms of hitting or exceeding pro forma.

So as you look at the plan for next year, I think we have a lot of confidence in that because we're essentially doing all infill locations where the visibility is just much higher.

Leah Jordan: And then for my follow-up, I know there's been some discussion around the puts and takes around gross margin, but the Street is expecting expansion as we look ahead to '27. I know you're not providing guidance today. You kind of brought in the expectations for 4Q a bit. I'm just trying to gain comfort in your view on gross margin expansion potential into next year. We've got some cost increases rising. I'm thinking about, typically, you guys have lagged, and there's always kind of a hit, and then you catch up. Is that really still the dynamic we should think about? Or the timing and ability to pass through?

And then, is there more pressure in the near-term from these input costs? Or are things like the op mix, more effective promotions, is that enough to kind of offset this interim period? I'm just trying to think about the next few quarters instead of just this stair-step change up.

Ian Ferry: Yes, fair question. Let me just start with Q4 and bridge you on that, and then I'll kind of move to '27. So, as you look at last year in Q4, we did about a 29.7% margin. This year, we're guiding to a 29.7% to 30.0%, and we will have about a 40 basis point benefit from just higher opportunistic mix flowing through. In addition, we'll probably see about 20 basis points of improvement on shrink. Now that will be partially offset by, call it, 40 basis points, give or take, of pressure on supply chain, which is predominantly fuel and freight, which is pronounced this year and certainly worse than our plan.

But netting all that out, we still expect at the midpoint to expand gross margins year-over-year in the fourth quarter, largely driven by the opportunistic mix improvement. Now, as we go to '27, you're right, we don't have a bottoms-up budget yet. We'll guide on the next call, but maybe I can provide a couple comments on the P&L that'd be helpful. In terms of comp growth, I mean, you've seen where we guided for Q4. We certainly expect that we can sustain that into next year. And on gross margins, which is your specific question, we will have the benefit of removing these synthetic promotions next year as we lap that and some of the store closure costs.

So, we do expect to see a year-over-year increase in gross margin for '27. Now, on the bottom half of the P&L with SG&A, there is likely to be some fixed cost pressure. And mainly I would point you to occupancy, where some of our locations that we're opening are in higher rent areas. And then an even bigger impact is just escalators on the large base moving through the system. And so, that will be a source of deleverage in the P&L. Where it all nets out, we'll update you in March. We do expect to have healthy growth and profitability each year as we move forward, but there will be some pressure on SG&A.

And then lastly, I would just point out, with the reduction in new stores for next year and some ongoing efficiencies, we will expect CapEx aggregate dollars to come down year-over-year, just as they had in 2026.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Next, we will move on to Simeon Gutman with Morgan Stanley.

Simeon Gutman: Jason, do you have a view on the overall mix of op versus every day when, I guess, the dust settles? When you started, you kind of identified places in everyday where you needed to enhance the selection. And do you think that is holding back the basket size? Or is it opportunistic that can end up driving the basket size higher?

Jason Potter: Yes, Simeon. Thanks for the question. So when you're thinking about the business, and we're looking at the mix and we're looking at SKU count, you also need to make sure that the customer has coverage in certain categories with assortment. So, it's a balancing act, but generally, I would just say that we got too off-balance with too much everyday assortment and not enough opportunistic product.

We think that by rebalancing that in the way we have and the work we still have in front of us, that we're going to have a nice everyday assortment that is going to cover the things we need to drive basket for loyal customers, but an exciting, high-turn opportunistic assortment that drives value for the customer. And one kind of salient point to make when you're thinking about mix, there's also, and I haven't talked about this before, but everyday product turns at a certain rate, and that's important for everyday baskets, it's important for certain missions. But we do list tens of thousands of op SKUs.

And so, they turn at a relatively higher rate than the balance of the business. So, there is that newness piece as well as the number of SKUs is important. And so, we're looking at that kind of holistically as we move the business forward. And so, I know that isn't a perfect answer, but we think that, again, just to underline, we got too far in front of ourselves on everyday assortments, whether that be private label or made-to-order product, and rebalancing that, we found, has been highly effective, and we're going to continue on that path.

Simeon Gutman: Okay. You mentioned October running good without promotion. I assume the Thanksgiving, that one has not begun yet. Can you just talk about the logic with Thanksgiving? Do you think it's defensive table stakes, you have to be there? Or are you seeing like these promotions are bringing in new customers and you're able to retain and bring them into the flywheel?

Jason Potter: Yes, no, great question. So, just again to reinforce, we're not going to continue to promote like a traditional retailer. The synthetic bridge we put in place is over. It's all about op. As you pointed out, we did not have these synthetic promotions in October, and I would just tell you again that comps ran at the high end of the range. So, we're feeling good about the underlying performance and value excitement that's generating. Just given the promotional environment, we're making a surgical bet over and above our regular investment for Thanksgiving. And Thanksgiving is really important. We didn't get it quite right last year.

And so, getting value right during this critical selling period reinforces our positioning, and it creates engagement with our most loyal customers right through the quarter and beyond, and there is a component of new customer attraction that does happen. Now, all of that to say, that's all in our guidance. We're going to remain disciplined but flexible. We're managing the competitive price gaps, we're monitoring the environment, and we, at times, will make informed bets that are surgical, but nothing systematic like we did earlier in the year.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the call back to Jason Potter for closing remarks. I'm sorry, there is somebody that just queued up. Would you like to take that question?

Operator: We'll hear from Joe Feldman with Telsey Advisory Group.

Joseph Feldman: Sorry. I guess, I didn't hit the star one early enough earlier. Question about, you said you guys are seeing new customers, which is terrific, and I'm wondering a couple things. What's drawing them in? And also, are you seeing them repeat after initial visitation?

Jason Potter: Yes, great question, Joe. Thanks for asking it. We are seeing new customers when we look at our credit card data. What's driving them in is our -- the value we're creating through op. We're seeing that in the underlying data, and they are repeating. So, you always manage and you're watching things like customer churn. We're looking at the credit card data as a proxy to understand that, and what we can see right now is that strategy is working and is on point. And again, another reason why we believe that the continued work here is essential and will continue right through next year.

Joseph Feldman: So, it's the ops helping to drive it, and that message is getting out. I guess, the other question I did have was, when you guys talked about the stores, I know you've closed a bunch of the stores already, the 36 stores. Did you share how much of a headwind that was in the quarter? I was just curious how much pressure it was on total sales, if you could share.

Ian Ferry: Yes, we didn't, but it's probably roughly $30 million.

Joseph Feldman: Got it. Okay, yes, it's just helpful to understand because the growth is, the comp is certainly much better and it looks good.

Operator: And there are no further questions. I would now like to turn the call back to Jason Potter for closing remarks.

Jason Potter: Once again, we appreciate the questions. Thanks for your engagement on the call. And we'll see some of you a little later today. Thank you so much for attending.

Operator: Thank you. This does conclude today's teleconference. We thank you for your participation. You may disconnect your lines at this time.

#2996. Sonos (SONO) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management details margin targets and memory cost pressures ahead.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Sonos, Inc. (SONO -0.70%) returned to top-line growth in fiscal 2026, driven by a series of hardware launches and the introduction of a next-generation software platform. Management reported that annual revenue increased 7% to $1,546.9 million, while adjusted EBITDA rose 39% as the company realized structural improvements in profitability. The company introduced five new products during the year, including headphones and home cinema components, while transitioning to an annual fall release cadence for its system software. Despite significant headwinds from elevated memory prices, management indicated that component mitigation efforts and pricing adjustments remain on track to deliver approximately 500 basis points of annualized margin improvement by the end of fiscal 2027. The company is prioritizing its installer channel and direct-to-consumer platform to maximize higher-margin sales opportunities.

Operator: Good day, everyone, and welcome to the Sonos Fourth Quarter and Fiscal 26 Conference Call. Please note that today's call is being recorded. At this time, I will hand the call over to mister James Baglanis. Head of corporate finance. Please go ahead, sir.

James Baglanis: Good afternoon, and welcome to Sonos Fourth Quarter and Fiscal 26 Earnings Conference Call. I am James Baglanis, with me today are Sonos' CEO, Thomas Conrad; CFO, Saori Casey; chief legal officer, Eddie Lazarus. Before I hand it over to Thomas Conrad, I would like to remind everyone that today's discussion will include forward-looking statements regarding future events and our future financial performance. These statements reflect our views as of today only and should not be considered as representing our views of any subsequent date. These statements are also subject to material risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from the expectations reflected in the forward-looking statements.

A discussion of these risk factors is fully detailed under the caption Risk" in our filings with the SEC. During this call, we will also refer to certain non GAAP financial measures. For information regarding our non GAAP financials and a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP measures, please refer to today's press release regarding our fourth quarter and fiscal 26 results posted to the Investor Relations portion of our website. investors.sonos.com. After the call concludes, we will upload our revised supplemental earnings presentation including our guidance, as well as our conference call transcript to the IR website. I will now turn the call over to Thomas Conrad.

#2992. Federal Reserve Board requests public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

#2985. NextNav (NN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Debt-free balance sheet and a SpaceX spectrum deal frame NextNav's regulatory push.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

NextNav Inc. (NN -5.83%) reported significant progress in its regulatory and technical objectives during the third quarter, supported by a substantially strengthened balance sheet following the elimination of all corporate debt. Management indicated that market validation for low-band spectrum assets has intensified, citing a proposed acquisition of spectrum by SpaceX as a key precedent for the scarcity value of these resources. The company continues to advance its proposal for a terrestrial Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) system as a complement to GPS, which is currently undergoing an interagency review process facilitated by the Federal Communications Commission. Management stated that the core issues of PNT resiliency and national security maintain strong bipartisan support as the regulatory process moves into 2027.

Mariam Sorond: Thank you, Jared. Good afternoon, and thank you all for joining us today. The third quarter was productive on all fronts, marked by continued regulatory progress, important technical milestones, new partnerships and perhaps most notably, highly visible market validation of the increasing value and strategic importance low-band spectrum assets. The proposed acquisition of Grain's low band spectrum assets by SpaceX defines an important market precedent, which highlights the finite nature and scarcity value of low-band spectrum. We believe this creates an increasingly constructive backdrop for our long-term opportunity and further validates the trend we have discussed for some time.

As demand for low band spectrum continues to grow, we believe there is an urgency to ensure these finite resources are maximized in support of the public interest. Beyond the transaction, we were particularly pleased to see SpaceX file 2 ex-parte letters referencing our lower 900 megahertz proposal. We believe these filings reflect growing industry recognition that additional low-band spectrum will be needed to support next-generation connectivity services. Furthermore, we believe the filings underscore the significant value that can be unlocked by putting these scarce spectrum resources to productive use in the near future.

Among other things, SpaceX urged the FCC to encourage fast investments to put scarce low- and mid-band spectrum to use, including for innovative services like terrestrial, direct-to-device and IoT services. Further, on the regulatory front, as we have discussed previously, the FCC has formally submitted a draft notice of proposed rule-making or NPRM focused on promoting the development of PNT technologies and solutions for an interagency review process. And now with the midterm election behind us, it is important to reiterate that the core issues underpinning this proceeding, including PNT's resiliency, national security, critical infrastructure protection, economic security and public safety have consistently received bipartisan support.

We continue to work with the administration and the FCC and are well positioned to engage constructively with the new Congress to advance a ground-based complement and backup to GPS as the process advances. While differing viewpoints are a standard feature of major spectrum proceedings, our team continues to engage extensively across the federal government and with key stakeholders, leveraging every appropriate avenue to equip decision-makers with engineering and data-driven analysis to advance the process. We believe they have resulted in meaningful progress within the administration and various federal agencies. We also continue to engage constructively and have conversations with users in the band, including key industries such as railroad operators, tolling and other industry stakeholders.

We seek to resolve coexistence matters through a fact-based approach that relies on testing and demonstrations. Notably, we concluded testing with the freight rail industry where we have been conducting real-world collaborative testing and detailed discussions on coexistence. Further, we have been holding early conversations with additional stakeholders in the band to develop appropriate test plans that will satisfy their systems and operational needs. NextNav continues to collaborate on coexistence testing and we have illustrated how our 5G PNT and sensing solutions can benefit their operations. Our team continues to engage with the public safety community as we advance our 5G-powered 3D location technology to meet their needs.

To date, we have engaged with Fire, Police and 911 officials across the country to advance indoor positioning capabilities that will enhance emergency response and first responder safety. These efforts have included discussions with Fairfax County, Arlington County, Phoenix, Philadelphia and Plano fire departments, North Central Texas 911 and the International Association of Firefighters. Commercially, we have been strategic in assembling the building blocks needed to enable new applications on our spectrum, including 5G capable PNT and sensing technologies designed to operate on standardized 5G networks. On positioning, we have partnered with Safran on timing with Oscilloquartz. And through our partnership with Tiami and AiRANACULUS, we are extending our capabilities into long-range sensing.

Together, these partnerships demonstrate the growing range of applications that can be deployed on spectrum including for national security, critical infrastructure and public safety. Specifically with Tiami, a recognized leader in drone sensing, we are showing how their existing capabilities can be integrated with NextNav signaling and deployed on our low-band spectrum. Importantly, this work highlights how sensing applications can operate on standardized 5G networks using our spectrum, creating a path towards scalable deployment of wide-area sensing capabilities. With AiRANACULUS, we are combining our technology and spectrum with our advanced signal processing, machine learning and AI capabilities to improve detection, identification and tracking of multiple drones over long distances.

What's key is that NextNav uniquely brings together the combination of the spectrum and technology capabilities needed to enable a wide-area long-range sensing solution at scale, including with sensing applications directly relevant to national security. Moreover, as these building blocks come together, we believe they expand the range of high-value applications that can be deployed on our spectrum. Separately, we achieved important technological validation milestones through real-world deployment and testing. Since early this year, we have been operating in Santa Clara County, California, under an experimental license utilizing the proposed band configuration and transmitting on a live 5G network environment.

These activities provide a real-world opportunity to validate our solution and further support the extensive technical analysis already on the record. Notably, we recently announced field testing results showing single-digit-meter positioning performance for both indoor and outdoor. This includes accurate positioning that can serve as a backup and also a complement to GPS in areas where GPS is challenged. Importantly, throughout our testing in Santa Clara, there has not been a single claim of interference. The demand for finite low-band spectrum continues to grow as the range of applications expand across wireless carriers, satellite operators and D2D providers as well as critical infrastructure, public safety and national security use cases. Timothy Horan: The California trial, does that kind of simulate real-world conditions for let's say, those get built out as part of a 5G network, what a carrier would do in terms of power and coverage or in-building penetration? Yes.

Mariam Sorond: Thank you, Tim, for the question. The 5G network in Santa Clara operating on 5G towers for both the base station and device on 5G towers. So it is very much a real-world situation of how you would do PNT in a 5G network. It's showing and demonstrating the technology. I invite everyone to come visit us in Santa Clara. To see how we provide the accuracy that is needed for the complement and backup proposal that we are, it works great.

Timothy Horan: And I know you said there's been no reports of interference, but have you done maybe more extensive or intensive trials yourself to see if there was any interference?

Mariam Sorond: The Santa Clara network is to demonstrate that we are meeting a national security environment. But obviously, we are transmitting at full 5G powers across the base station and the device. So we have not heard the way that the STA is set up is that it allows anyone in the band to call with an interference issue. We've not had any.

Timothy Horan: Okay. And then are you hearing -- is there any -- or when do you think the next band of sub-1 gigahertz spectrum can be freed up other than yourself at this point? You just -- curious if you're hearing any.

Mariam Sorond: I really can't speculate on what other spectrum could be in the pipeline that would free up it would need to be going through a regulatory process and a clearing process similar to what was done, for example, when we saw the incentive auction happen in 600 megahertz. So, if there is new spectrum to be coming up the regulatory process, we'll need to follow very closely. And the same time lines that we saw over there.

So low band continues on the -- to be very scarce currently, especially as we see this market dynamics of needing low band for the new entrants and even the existing players, I believe that the short term is really what's available out there.

Timothy Horan: And then lastly, are you continuing to have conversations with the FCC? And have you had any conversations with OIRA? Do you have any sense what the delay is at this point? I know you said you're making -- in the earnings release, you're making progress on the regulatory front. I guess if you could elaborate on that would be great.

Mariam Sorond: We continue to talk to the administration and all the federal agencies. So -- and as we can see, there are folks who are going to see the OIRA and they have to manage their process. They have to hear out everyone and then they have to be able to ask their questions that they need. So we're working constructively with everyone as this process continues.

Timothy Horan: Got it. So you think it's just a matter of everyone interacting with OIRA and expressing what their concerns are and then OIRA ultimately making that decision?

Mariam Sorond: Yes. I think the whole purpose of the OIRA process is designed to allow interested parties to present their views. And we're not surprised that our opponents are using this interagency process especially since the FCC sent the NPRM out. Some parties are slower than others to have their meetings, but it's continuing.

Timothy Horan: Do you have any sense on the timing where they are in the process? Have they met with everyone at this point?

Mariam Sorond: We have -- we're not going to disclose a sense of timing because this is a process that is managed by OMB and OIRA and how they see this and who else might want to talk to it is really their process, so I can't comment on their timing.

Operator: Your next question comes from Greg Pendy with Clear Street.

Unknown Analyst: Can you just remind us -- I know the recent rail data came out, but is there any other coexistence data or test results that you'll be submitting to the FCC on record to address any of the other opposition filings out there?

Mariam Sorond: Thank you for the question. I think we have put a substantial amount of coexistence data, the FCC has sent the NPRM, we believe we have shown the path to move forward. As part of the NPRM process, the FCC may require further analysis or more data, and we would be working with them to make sure that we provide that when it's needed.

Operator: Your next question comes from David Joyce with Seaport Research Partners.

David Joyce: With the broader satellite and wireless competitive landscape in flux attention has obviously been drawn to the potential for direct-to-device use cases. You did allude to that earlier. But what testing, if any, have you done on that front? What other elements would need to be in place for you to see if there's any progress that can be made there?

Mariam Sorond: Thank you for the question. I think our focus has been on PNT and our testing has been our terrestrial PNT. But of course, I think in the D2D space, there is existing testing on low-band spectrum that has been done. I think that testing is a validation of what it can do. I don't think it needs to be reproduced. And I think the stakeholders are interested in it, who have access to their own test data to be able to tell what the performance is on low band. We're focused on PRS and PNT because that is a new capability that has not been demonstrated and tested.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time, and that concludes the NextNav Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#2982. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Federal Reserve Board today published feedback letters for resolution plans submitted in October 2025. The agencies did not identify any shortcomings or deficiencies in these resolution plan submissions.

Resolution plans, also known as living wills, describe a banking organization's strategy for orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure. The agencies conducted a joint review of the 2025 resolution plan submissions from 15 banking organizations with over $250 billion in assets.

In addition, the agencies determined that the shortcoming previously identified in the 2021 BNP Paribas resolution plan has been satisfactorily addressed.

#2980. Shift4: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Subscription revenue fell 10% as Shift4 traded legacy software fees for payment volume, a trade whose payoff for shareholders remains unproven.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Shift4 (FOUR -2.84%) announced $200 million in quarterly adjusted free cash flow, the cash remaining after paying operating costs and capital expenses. For long-term investors, the payment processing company continues to show that its core payments revenue can expand even when macroeconomic turbulence impacts specific merchant categories. Three takeaways from the call explain where the business stands today.

Shift4 generated $200 million in quarterly adjusted free cash flow, which measures core cash generation after capital investments. Management put that cash to work by purchasing its own stock at levels it considers deeply discounted. The company has repurchased nearly a quarter of its shares since its initial public offering, when a private company first sells shares to the public. Management also announced a new $1 billion share repurchase authorization, effective in 2027.

Subscription and other revenue fell 10% year over year as management intentionally phased out legacy software fees. The company uses software price breaks to move merchants onto its main transaction processing platform, exchanging smaller fixed fees for larger recurring payment flows. Shift4 Dine, the company's flagship restaurant software, now powers more than half of its restaurant clients, thereby extending customer lifetime value and building long-term payment volume.

International payments revenue surged 31% year over year despite ongoing travel disruptions in the Middle East that weighed on cross-border tourism. Shift4 One, the company's single payment terminal that combines transaction processing, currency conversion, and tax refunds, is now live in 15 countries. That expanding footprint supports Global Blue, the tax-free shopping business Shift4 acquired to capture high-margin tourist spending across global luxury retail.

Software-integrated payment adoption outside North America remains in its infancy, giving Shift4 an early-mover edge across international markets. The company relies on its broad presence across hotels, sports venues, and luxury retail while keeping net leverage, which compares net debt to core earnings, below 3.8 times. Management is watching total merchant processing costs and international travel recovery patterns.

Long-term execution relies on compounding payments revenue across new markets while expanding profit margins as global integrations finish.

#2976. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.
